utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Yes, and because they come back, detention can be reserved for the few truly dangerous defendants.

utterances.speaker: Javier
utterances.text: My own county ended cash bail for most misdemeanor charges last spring.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Professional basketball teams should be required to disclose players' injury details before every game because pre-game injury information helps spectators understand which players are available and how the game may unfold.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A team's injury report can change opponents' preparation shortly before a game. For that reason, consistent pre-game disclosure is necessary for fair preparation by both teams.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Another reason for requiring disclosure is that a league-wide rule would prevent teams from gaining an advantage by withholding injury information.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The rule would make competition fairer because the same information would be available to every team before the game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Mandatory injury disclosure can expose sensitive medical information and pressure injured players to return. That objection matters, but it does not outweigh the case for a carefully limited requirement.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I usually watch televised games with a notebook nearby.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, teams should have to publish players' injury details before every game.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A league-wide requirement would stop teams from selectively concealing injuries, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A clear reporting template could limit the amount of medical information that teams publish because it could not balance competitive transparency with player privacy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A pre-game report can distinguish a confirmed absence from a player's uncertain status.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, pre-game injury reporting can separate confirmed absences from uncertain player statuses.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The disclosure rule should allow updates when a player's condition changes after the initial report.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To put that differently, the disclosure rule should permit revised reports when a player's condition changes.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether councils should make landlords fit basic energy-efficiency measures before a rental licence can be renewed. Priya, you first.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Councils should make that a condition of renewal, because tenants in cold, poorly insulated homes pay hundreds of pounds more every winter.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: But landlords will simply pass the cost on through higher rents.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Alejandro, you are saying tenants would end up paying for the upgrades anyway.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Grants cover most of the cost of the upgrades, so the burden on landlords is small. That is another reason to make the work a licence condition.

utterances.speaker: Alejandro
utterances.text: The council's licensing team has only four inspectors, so checking every property would overwhelm them.

utterances.speaker: Priya
utterances.text: Which is to say, Emeka, that landlords would carry little of the expense. And the scheme has been running since 2019, so the team knows the properties.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Put another way, Alejandro, the council could not police the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Landlords who upgraded saw fewer empty months between tenants, which shows upgrades pay for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take audience votes after the break.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should force every electric car onto one charging standard. Josefa, you start.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Governments should require one universal standard, because drivers can't currently be sure a public charger will fit their car.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: But a mandate would freeze the technology in place, since better connectors are still being developed.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Drivers can't be sure because three different plug types are in common use on public networks.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Theo, you run charging stations. What do you see?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: My company operates two hundred stations. Fitting several plug types at every site raises our installation costs.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So, Theo, you are saying that supporting several plug types makes stations more expensive to build.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Exactly. A single standard would lower prices for drivers, because stations would need to fit only one connector.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I'll put my point another way: a mandate would lock in today's connector for fifteen years or more.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Darius is saying that today's connector would be fixed for fifteen years or more, and that is the reason to accept that a mandate would lock it in.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Yes, and charging speeds have doubled in five years, which shows connectors are still improving. I should add that I only charge at home myself.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is the end of tonight's debate.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should force every electric car onto one charging standard. Josefa, you start.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Drivers can't currently be sure a public charger will fit their car, because governments should require one universal standard.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: But a mandate would freeze the technology in place, since better connectors are still being developed.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Drivers can't be sure because three different plug types are in common use on public networks.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Theo, you run charging stations. What do you see?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Fitting several plug types at every site raises our installation costs.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So, Theo, you are saying that supporting several plug types makes stations more expensive to build.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Exactly. Separately, a single standard would lower prices for drivers, because stations would need to fit only one connector.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I'll put my point another way: a mandate would lock in today's connector for fifteen years or more.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying today's connector would be fixed for fifteen years or more.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Yes, and the number of connector designs in testing has tripled in five years, which shows connectors are still improving. I should add that I only charge at home myself.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is the end of tonight's debate.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Retailers sometimes use colored labels on fresh-produce packaging.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay such a levy because unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce creates disposal costs for local authorities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why should the levy focus specifically on unnecessary packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Much fresh produce does not need extra plastic packaging to remain saleable, which is why the levy is justified. I learned to judge the ripeness of fruit from my grandmother.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that retailers should pay the levy on unnecessary plastic packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers can redesign their packaging quickly. Because of that, retailers can avoid the levy by removing unnecessary packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Who would actually bear the charge?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy would be billed to retailers rather than shoppers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some retailers warn that the measure would make food more expensive.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A levy on unnecessary packaging would raise retail prices, but that objection does not outweigh the case for the levy.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The price increase caused by the levy would be modest. Levy revenue could finance grants for reducing packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, the levy would produce only a modest increase in prices.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy should be simple to administer, because a clear definition of unnecessary packaging would make enforcement straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A clear definition would distinguish protective packaging from packaging used merely for presentation.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Existing packaging records would make enforcement of the levy practical because retailers already record the materials used in their packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, in other words, your proposal is for a levy that is straightforward to administer.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is your final reason for supporting the measure?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy should be introduced because its revenue could finance packaging-reduction grants.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should retailers pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers should pay a levy on unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce at a moderate rate because unnecessary plastic packaging around fresh produce creates disposal costs for local authorities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Why should the levy focus specifically on unnecessary packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Much fresh produce does not need extra plastic packaging to remain saleable, which is why the levy is justified. I learned to judge the ripeness of fruit from my grandmother.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that retailers should pay the levy on unnecessary plastic packaging?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers can redesign their packaging quickly. Because of that, retailers can avoid the levy by removing unnecessary packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Who would actually bear the charge?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy would be billed to retailers rather than shoppers.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some retailers warn that the measure would make food more expensive.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A levy on unnecessary packaging would raise retail prices, but that objection does not outweigh the case for the levy.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The price increase caused by the levy would be modest. Levy revenue could finance grants for reducing packaging.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, the levy would produce only a modest increase in prices.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy should be simple to administer, because a clear definition of unnecessary packaging would make enforcement straightforward.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A clear definition would distinguish protective packaging from packaging used merely for presentation.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Retailers already record the materials used in their packaging, so those existing packaging records would make enforcement of the levy practical.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So, in other words, your proposal is for a levy that is straightforward to administer.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is your final reason for supporting the measure?

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: The levy should be introduced because its revenue could finance packaging-reduction grants.

utterances.text: We are considering whether part of annual bonuses should be paid in company shares. Lars, please begin with the case for the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Employees who hold company shares benefit financially when the company succeeds. Because of that stake, employee share ownership gives employees a reason to stay with the company.

utterances.text: Because employees gain when the company succeeds, and because share ownership encourages retention, the company should replace part of annual bonuses with company shares.

utterances.text: Cash bonuses provide employees with predictable income, however, so I do not support replacing part of the bonus with shares. Separately, employees may find company shares difficult to value.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: In other words, employee ownership lets employees benefit financially from the company's success.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: To put the proposal plainly, the company would pay part of annual bonuses in company shares.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: The compensation committee meets again next Thursday, so we can discuss the valuation issue then.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: The company has reviewed several bonus designs this year.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Many elderly and unbanked people have no cards, because cashless shops should be required to take cash.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: But a mandate would burden small businesses with cash-handling costs.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Those costs are real, since you need safes, insurance and bank deposit fees. Also, our local cafe went cashless last spring.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Another reason for the rule is that cash still works when the card network is down.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying cashless shops shut out people who have no cards, which is why the rule is needed.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Put another way, the rule would hit small shops hardest.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Large chains can easily absorb the cost of handling cash, so the rule is workable.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I run a market stall that is mostly card-based.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Cashless shops should be required to take cash, because many elderly and unbanked people have no cards.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: But a mandate would burden small businesses with cash-handling costs.

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying cashless shops shut out people who have no cards, which is why the rule is needed.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: Put another way, the rule would hit small shops hardest.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Large chains can easily absorb the cost of handling cash, so the rule is workable.

utterances.speaker: Vikram
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I run a market stall that is mostly card-based.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether governments should automatically register every eligible citizen to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal; make the case.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Automatic registration would remove the paperwork that currently prevents some eligible citizens from registering, because governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I have not missed any national election. Automatic registration would not require citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But governments should not automatically register eligible citizens to vote. I moved three times during the last decade.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would place eligible citizens on the electoral rolls without requiring them to apply.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Carmen raises the problem of inaccurate records, while Beatriz points to people who are left out. How could the system stay current?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records. That is another reason to adopt automatic registration.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying that a national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Automatic registration would increase turnout among eligible citizens. That is a further reason why the increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But automatic registration would not guarantee informed participation in elections. Higher turnout by itself is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Put another way, automatic registration would leave the choice to vote entirely with each citizen.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Would either of you support safeguards such as an easy opt-out?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Because automatic registration would not require citizens to vote, automatic registration would separate registration from the act of voting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: An opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Privacy objections should not block automatic registration, because an opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Election offices would need to audit address data every year under an automatic registration system.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, an automatic registration system would require annual audits of address data by election offices.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: That reminder would make the new registration process easier for citizens to use, because a reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether governments should automatically register every eligible citizen to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal; make the case.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Automatic registration would remove the paperwork that currently prevents some eligible citizens from registering, because governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I have never missed a national election. Automatic registration would not require citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But governments should not automatically register eligible citizens to vote. I moved three times during the last decade.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would place eligible citizens on the electoral rolls without requiring them to apply.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Carmen raises the problem of inaccurate records, while Beatriz points to people who are left out. How could the system stay current?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records. That is another reason to adopt automatic registration.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying that a national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Automatic registration would increase turnout among eligible citizens. That is a further reason why the increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But automatic registration would not guarantee informed participation in elections. Higher turnout by itself is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Put another way, automatic registration would leave the choice to vote entirely with each citizen.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Would either of you support safeguards such as an easy opt-out?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Because automatic registration would not require citizens to vote, automatic registration can preserve voluntary voting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: An opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Privacy objections should not block automatic registration, because an opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Election offices would need to audit address data every year under an automatic registration system.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, an automatic registration system would require annual audits of address data by election offices.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: That reminder would make the new registration process easier for citizens to use, because a reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether governments should automatically register every eligible citizen to vote. Beatriz, you support the proposal; make the case.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote, because automatic registration would remove the paperwork that currently prevents some eligible citizens from registering.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: I have never missed a national election. Automatic registration would not require citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But governments should not automatically register eligible citizens to vote. I moved three times during the last decade.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: In other words, automatic registration would place eligible citizens on the electoral rolls without requiring them to apply.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Carmen raises the problem of inaccurate records, while Beatriz points to people who are left out. How could the system stay current?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records, because governments should automatically register eligible citizens to vote.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Your claim, in other words, is that a national register could update voters' addresses through existing public records.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Automatic registration would increase turnout among eligible citizens. That is a further reason why the increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: But automatic registration would not guarantee informed participation in elections. Higher turnout by itself is not enough.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Put another way, automatic registration would leave the choice to vote entirely with each citizen.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: Would either of you support safeguards such as an easy opt-out?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: The increase in turnout would make automatic registration a worthwhile reform.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Because automatic registration would not require citizens to vote, automatic registration can preserve voluntary voting.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: An opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: Privacy objections should not block automatic registration, because an opt-out portal would let citizens remove themselves from the register.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Under an automatic registration system, election offices would have to audit address data annually.

utterances.speaker: Quentin
utterances.text: In other words, an automatic registration system would require annual audits of address data by election offices.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: A reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: That reminder would make the new registration process easier for citizens to use, because a reminder sent after registration would tell citizens where and when to vote.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should students have to demonstrate swimming proficiency before joining a competitive school sports team?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. Swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some coaches say that swimming has little to do with sports such as basketball or track. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams, because swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: That seems excessive to some families. They argue that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety in school sports and that a swimming requirement would unfairly exclude capable students from competitive teams.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, swimming competence is a basic safety condition for school sports. That position directly rejects the claim that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety. Put another way, schools should make swimming proficiency a condition for joining competitive sports teams; that position also rejects the claim that the requirement would unfairly exclude capable students.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: I learned to swim at a community pool, but my personal experience is not the main issue.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because swimming competence is a basic safety condition, a requirement would give coaches confidence that team members can respond safely to an accidental fall into water.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Since swimming competence is a basic safety condition, the requirement would encourage students to learn a practical life skill before representing their schools.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The interview is being recorded for the school newsletter. Would you apply the rule immediately?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should offer affordable swimming lessons before enforcing the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The requirement should also be humane. Since schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should allow temporary exemptions for students with medical restrictions on swimming.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Finally, because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should assess it through a basic safety test rather than competitive racing.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should students have to demonstrate swimming proficiency before joining a competitive school sports team?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Yes. Swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Some coaches say that swimming has little to do with sports such as basketball or track. What is your response?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Schools should require swimming proficiency before students join competitive sports teams, because swimming competence is important for protecting students during school sports activities.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: That seems excessive to some families. They argue that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety in school sports and that a swimming requirement would unfairly exclude capable students from competitive teams.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: In other words, swimming competence is a basic safety condition for school sports. That position directly rejects the claim that swimming proficiency has no relevance to safety. Put another way, schools should make swimming proficiency a condition for joining competitive sports teams; that position also rejects the claim that the requirement would unfairly exclude capable students.

utterances.text: I prefer swimming in indoor pools.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The school team's swim caps are blue.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because swimming competence is a basic safety condition, a requirement would give coaches confidence that team members can respond safely to an accidental fall into water.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Since swimming competence is a basic safety condition, the requirement would encourage students to learn a practical life skill before representing their schools.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The same safety principle is another reason for requiring swimming proficiency: it would create a common safety standard across different competitive sports teams.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: The interview is being recorded for the school newsletter. Would you apply the rule immediately?

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should offer affordable swimming lessons before enforcing the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: The requirement should also be humane. Since schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should allow temporary exemptions for students with medical restrictions on swimming.

utterances.speaker: Keiko
utterances.text: Finally, because schools should make proficiency a condition of team entry, schools should assess it through a basic safety test rather than competitive racing.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Federations should impose salary caps, because caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But federations have no business setting wages, since pay is negotiated between clubs and the players' unions.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Without a cap the wealthiest clubs can outbid everyone else for every top player, which is why balance needs one. Attendance also falls when the same club wins every year, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I spent twelve years working in club academies. In capped North American leagues, ten different clubs won the title in fifteen years, which shows that caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Bernard, you are saying that under caps the titles get spread around.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: But capped leagues lose their stars, because foreign clubs pay far more.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: So you are saying that salary caps send talent abroad. Incidentally, our national league introduced its cap in 2011.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, can the union objection be answered?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Caps can be set through collective agreements with the unions, so federations can impose them. Broadcasters also pay more for tight title races, which is a further reason caps work.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: In other words, the domestic league would lose its best players to other leagues, and that matters because broadcast income follows the stars.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: Put another way, without a cap money alone would decide who wins. And clubs in capped leagues invest more in their youth academies, which is another reason for balance.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should national federations impose salary caps on professional leagues? Rafael, you start.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Federations should impose salary caps, because caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Ivana, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But federations have no business setting wages, since pay is negotiated between clubs and the players' unions.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Without a cap the wealthiest clubs can outbid everyone else for every top player, which is why balance needs one. Attendance also falls when the same club wins every year, which is another reason.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, what does the evidence say?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: I spent twelve years working in club academies. In capped North American leagues, ten different clubs won the title in fifteen years, which shows that caps keep competition balanced.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Bernard, you are saying that under caps the titles get spread around.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: But capped leagues lose their stars, because foreign clubs pay far more.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: So you are saying that salary caps send talent abroad. Incidentally, our national league introduced its cap in 2011.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Bernard, can the union objection be answered?

utterances.speaker: Bernard
utterances.text: Since, as I said, under caps the titles get spread around, caps can be set through collective agreements with the unions, so federations can impose them. Broadcasters also pay more for tight title races, which is a further reason caps work.

utterances.speaker: Ivana
utterances.text: In other words, the domestic league would lose its best players to other leagues, and that matters because broadcast income follows the stars.

utterances.speaker: Rafael
utterances.text: Put another way, without a cap money alone would decide who wins.

utterances.speaker: Daniela

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: For context, I returned a pair of shoes last week.

utterances.text: Many physical shops already have counters and staff for processing returns. Because that existing shop capacity is available, processing online returns is feasible.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Physical shops could process online returns without major structural changes. Because of that, existing shop capacity makes processing online returns feasible.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Some customers live too far from a participating physical shop to use it conveniently. That is why a shop-return expectation could exclude those customers.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The policy would not require every shop to accept every online purchase.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: So you mean that the policy could not use a limited network of participating shops.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Returning an online purchase at a shop would be convenient for customers who already visit that shop, and that convenience is a reason to expect those customers to use the shops.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Because some customers live too far from participating shops, a shop-return expectation could exclude them.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether people should be expected to take online purchases back to physical shops. Daniela, you support that proposal.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Online retailers can provide prepaid return labels and clear instructions because people should be expected to return online purchases to physical shops.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Would that expectation also create duties for the retailers themselves?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Yes. Online retailers should provide prepaid return labels.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Retailers can generate those labels automatically, because they already hold the order details.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Generating prepaid return labels costs retailers very little, which is why automatic generation is practical.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: But requiring shop workers to process online returns would be unfair; the shops did not make the original sale.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal would shift the retailers' responsibility onto shop workers.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: For context, I returned a pair of shoes last week.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Many physical shops already have counters and staff for processing returns. Because that existing shop capacity is available, processing online returns is feasible.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Let's consider another point.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: Physical shops could process online returns without major structural changes.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Some customers live too far from a participating physical shop to use it conveniently. That is why a shop-return expectation could exclude those customers.

utterances.speaker: Selin
utterances.text: The policy would not require every shop to accept every online purchase.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: So you mean that the policy could use a limited network of participating shops.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Returning an online purchase at a shop would be convenient for customers who already visit that shop, and that convenience is a reason to expect those customers to use the shops.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Because some customers live too far from participating shops, a shop-return expectation could exclude them.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: The studio audience has been unusually quiet tonight. We will take the final statements after the break.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Item two: whether the government should pay towards satellite internet for homes with no reliable broadband. Seamus, you start.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I say yes, we should subsidise it, because laying fibre to remote farms would cost far more per household than a satellite subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Satellite is only a stopgap, and it locks households into a private provider.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: My cousin runs a sheep farm and still uses a dial-up line.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: That is why I say the subsidy would simply hand public money to one company, since a stopgap that locks people in benefits only the provider.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: But the money would go to households, not the company, and they could spend it on any approved provider.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying it works like a voucher that households can use anywhere approved.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Sorry, the projector has been flickering all morning, can someone look at it?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Also, rural children without reliable internet fall behind in schoolwork that is set online, which is a reason to act.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: In other words, with online homework a home connection is essential for pupils.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Then let us do a pilot subsidy in two rural districts for a year.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: That is to say, a small trial before we commit to a national scheme.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Restorative conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences, because a court record follows a teenager into every job application.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But that ignores the victims, many of whom want a trial and a formal finding of guilt.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: On the contrary, victims who attend conferences rarely regret it, since they get answers they would never hear in court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Offenders may fake remorse to escape a trial, so conferences will be expensive to run and will burden already stretched community services.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Not quite: faked remorse is hard to sustain in a conference, because the victim describes the damage straight to your face.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: I coached youth football for years, as it happens. Put differently, you think the meeting itself exposes false remorse.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Reoffending is lower after conferences than after prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Lower by how much?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The proof is that pilot schemes saw about a fifth fewer repeat offences, and the reason is that offenders must face the harm they caused.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The pilots were small and carefully chosen, which is why that fifth may not carry over to a national scheme.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put differently, the pilot result might not hold nationally. I read those reports on a long train journey, so I did have time to notice.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly, in other words the pilot evidence is too thin to rely on.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Restorative conferences should replace prosecution for selected juvenile offences, because a court record follows a teenager into every job application.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: But that ignores the victims, many of whom want a trial and a formal finding of guilt.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: On the contrary, victims who attend conferences rarely regret it, since they get answers they would never hear in court.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Offenders may fake remorse to escape a trial, so conferences cannot be trusted to change behaviour.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Not quite: faked remorse is hard to sustain in a conference, because the victim describes the damage straight to your face.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Put differently, you think the meeting itself exposes false remorse.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Yes. Reoffending is lower after conferences than after prosecution, which is another reason to replace prosecution for these cases.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Lower by how much?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The proof is that pilot schemes saw about a fifth fewer repeat offences, and the reason is that offenders must face the harm they caused.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: The pilots were small and carefully chosen, which is why that fifth may not carry over to a national scheme.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put differently, the pilot result might not hold nationally. I read those reports on a long train journey, so I did have time to notice.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly, in other words the pilot evidence is too thin to rely on.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments ban the release of genetically modified mosquitoes? Aiko, you start.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Governments should ban these releases, because the ecological consequences simply cannot be predicted.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Aiko, governments should prohibit these releases outright.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: Releasing modified mosquitoes is an effective way to control dengue, since trial releases cut local Aedes populations by over eighty percent.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: But the suppressed populations rebounded within two years once the releases stopped.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Helga, what about the cost side?

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Releases cost far more than bed nets, because each site needs a continuous supply of modified insects.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: In other words, Helga, bed nets are cheaper per case averted.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Communities should be consulted before any release, since the insects cross property lines.

utterances.speaker: Aiko
utterances.text: Regulators should require public registers of every release, because public trust depends on transparency.

utterances.speaker: Pablo
utterances.text: I spent three years working on the Brazil trials, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Gene drives are irreversible. Put another way, once one is released it cannot be recalled.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether online voting should be introduced for national elections. Alina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Yes, it should, because turnout among young people is low and getting to a polling station is a hassle for them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Adrian, is that convincing?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Estonia has run online voting for national elections for many years, I should add.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But online voting cannot be made secure enough for national elections, since a single hacked server could change the result without anyone noticing.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Astrid, do you see other problems?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Yes, someone could be pushed into casting their vote at home while a relative watches, which is another reason it is not secure.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Astrid, you are saying that online voting would make home voting open to family coercion.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Exactly. And public trust in the result would collapse after a single suspected breach, which shows the system cannot be secure enough.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: My own district had a polling station closed last year.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Online voting would also need a national digital identity system for every voter.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether online voting should be introduced for national elections. Alina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Alina
utterances.text: Yes, we ought to adopt internet voting in national elections, because turnout among young people is low and getting to a polling station is a hassle for them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Adrian, is that convincing?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Estonia has run online voting for national elections for many years, I should add.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: But online voting cannot be made secure enough for national elections, since a single hacked server could change the result without anyone noticing.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Astrid, do you see other problems?

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Yes, voters could be pressured to vote at home under a relative's eye, which is another reason it is not secure.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Astrid, you are saying that online voting would make home voting open to family coercion.

utterances.speaker: Astrid
utterances.text: Exactly. And public confidence in the result would collapse after one suspected breach, which shows the system cannot be secure enough.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: My own district had a polling station closed last year.

utterances.speaker: Rania
utterances.text: Separately, online voting would need a national digital identity system to work in any country.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because adults have authority over decisions about their own bodies.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Palliative care cannot relieve every kind of suffering, which is why the right matters. The reason is that pain stays uncontrolled for some patients even in the best hospices.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Critics object, though, that vulnerable people could be pressured into choosing death.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: That ignores the screening: it would detect most pressure on vulnerable patients, because a request would need approval from two doctors and a waiting period.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has run its law since 1997 without evidence of widespread abuse, which shows that the screening works.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I volunteered in a hospice for three years.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: No doctor would be obliged to take part. In other words, doctors could opt out.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The right should exist since anyone who dislikes the idea never has to ask for it. Put another way, it is an option, not an obligation.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Waiting periods help the screening work, because they give patients time to reconsider; that time matters since a patient can withdraw a request at any point.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: To put it differently, approval would be slow and double-checked. That is to say, dying people would still have a say in how their lives end.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: My grandmother passed away in 2015.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Agenda item two: should mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences be abolished? Emeka, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Yes, they should be abolished, because they take sentencing discretion away from judges.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Take the courier case: a judge must give a first-time courier the same term as a kingpin, since the minimum applies by the weight of the drugs and not by the defendant's role.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: But they deter drug dealing, because prosecutors can use the threat of a minimum to get defendants to testify against suppliers.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Studies find no fall in drug supply after minimums were introduced, which is another reason to abolish them.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying, Emeka, that minimums have not reduced the supply of drugs.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: For the record, I worked as a probation officer for six years.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A quick note: the room is booked only until five o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Leverage like that is another reason to abolish, since it pressures defendants who have a good defence into pleading guilty, because they fear long mandatory terms.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Without minimums, sentences would vary from judge to judge; in other words, identical offences would get very different terms.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Disparity already exists under minimums, because prosecutors decide which charge triggers one.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: In other words, the disparity moves from judges to prosecutors rather than disappearing, which is the reason why, as Wilhelmina says, without minimums sentences would vary from judge to judge. Let us note both views and move to the vote.

utterances.text: Yes, they should be abolished, because they take sentencing discretion away from judges.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Take the courier case: a judge must give a first-time courier the same term as a kingpin, since the minimum applies by the weight of the drugs and not by the defendant's role.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: But they discourage drug dealing, because prosecutors can use the threat of a minimum to get defendants to testify against suppliers.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Studies find no fall in drug supply after minimums were introduced, which is another reason to abolish them.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying, Emeka, that minimums have not reduced the supply of drugs.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: For the record, I worked as a probation officer for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A quick note: the room is booked only until five o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So what you mean, Wilhelmina, is that prosecutors use the threat of a minimum as a bargaining tool.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Leverage like that is another reason to abolish, since it pressures defendants who have a good defence into pleading guilty, because they fear long mandatory terms.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Without minimums, sentences would vary from judge to judge; in other words, identical offences would get very different terms.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Disparity already exists under minimums, because prosecutors decide which charge triggers one.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: In other words, the disparity moves from judges to prosecutors rather than disappearing. Let us note both views and move to the vote.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Agenda item two: should mandatory minimum sentences for drug offences be abolished? Emeka, would you open?

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Yes, they should be abolished, because they take sentencing discretion away from judges.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: But they deter drug dealing, because prosecutors can use the threat of a minimum to get defendants to testify against suppliers.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Studies find no fall in drug supply after minimums were introduced, which is another reason to abolish them.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So you are saying, Emeka, that minimums have not reduced the supply of drugs.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: For the record, I worked as a probation officer for six years.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A quick note: the room is booked only until five o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: So what you mean, Wilhelmina, is that prosecutors use the threat of a minimum as a bargaining tool.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Leverage like that is another reason to abolish, since it pressures defendants who have a good defence into pleading guilty; that is why defendants fear long mandatory terms and plead guilty to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: A judge must give a first-time courier the same term as a kingpin, since the minimum applies by the weight of the drugs and not by the defendant's role.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Without minimums, sentences would vary from judge to judge.

utterances.speaker: Emeka
utterances.text: Disparity already exists under minimums, because prosecutors decide which charge triggers one.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: In other words, the disparity moves from judges to prosecutors rather than disappearing. Let us note both views and move to the vote.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Without minimums, identical offences would receive very different terms.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Our question is whether employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement. Leilani, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Employers should publish salary ranges in every job advertisement. Salary ranges enable prospective applicants to determine before submitting an application whether the position fits their financial requirements.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: A substantial number of job advertisements stay posted for multiple weeks. That timing can make the recruitment process confusing.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: But mandatory salary ranges could discourage small employers from advertising vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Publishing salary ranges reduces the number of unsuitable applications, and hiring becomes more efficient when employers publish salary ranges.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: So you are saying that salary ranges reduce wasted applications. In other words, you are proposing a universal salary-range requirement for job advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Small employers often lack reliable data about prevailing salaries. Because of that, salary ranges published by small employers can be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Arjun, does that mean you reject salary transparency entirely?

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: No; because inaccurate ranges can mislead applicants, employers should be permitted to explain unusual salary ranges in their advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Published salary ranges can reveal arbitrary pay differences between comparable roles; that is another reason to support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: What you mean is that salary transparency can expose unjustified pay gaps.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Employers can give useful context for an unusual salary range in a short note. For that reason, the rule should allow explanatory notes alongside the range.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: For the record, my journey to the television studio took forty minutes today.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. Ayesha, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Merging neighbouring refuse-collection services would reduce administrative costs. The councils currently maintain separate billing, procurement, and management offices, so combining them would remove duplicated work.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I have worked on a municipal waste committee, but I am not convinced that a merger is automatically wise.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Some households put out extra garden waste after storms. That seasonal problem deserves attention even if the authorities keep their services separate.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Neighbouring councils already use compatible route-planning software. Because the software is compatible, a merged service could coordinate its depots.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Coordinated depots would reduce empty journeys by refuse vehicles. That is why the merger would also reduce administrative and operating costs.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But merging the services could make a failure at one depot disrupt collections across both councils. That risk is a serious objection to the cost-saving case.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: To put Felix's concern another way, a single depot failure could disrupt collections throughout the merged service.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Ayesha's central claim is that a merger would cut administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: An audit found that two councils saved twelve percent by jointly purchasing refuse bags and vehicle parts. That evidence supports merging the services because a larger authority could negotiate similar bulk discounts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. The administrative savings make that recommendation reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed policy is for neighbouring councils to operate one shared refuse-collection service. Felix, you will have a final response after the break.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: The neighbouring councils have not yet scheduled a vote on the refuse-collection proposal.

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. Ayesha, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Merging neighbouring refuse-collection services would reduce administrative costs. The councils currently maintain separate billing, procurement, and management offices, so combining them would remove duplicated work.

utterances.speaker: Felix

utterances.text: Ayesha's central claim is that a merger would cut administrative costs. Because this is her central claim, a merger would cut administrative costs.

utterances.text: An audit found that two councils saved twelve percent by jointly purchasing refuse bags and vehicle parts. That evidence supports merging the services because a larger authority could negotiate similar bulk discounts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. The administrative savings make that recommendation reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Free school breakfast would prevent many pupils from beginning lessons hungry, which is a strong reason for adopting the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason is that a universal breakfast would improve pupils' readiness to learn without requiring teachers to identify children in need.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Regular breakfast provision would help pupils attend school consistently; that practical benefit also supports providing the meal to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools already have the routines needed to distribute a morning meal efficiently, so this existing capacity is another reason to establish a universal programme.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing school kitchens could serve a nutritious breakfast without major new construction, which makes universal provision a realistic public-school responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal provision would prevent children from being singled out because their families receive assistance; that protection is another reason schools should adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A well-fed pupil is more likely to benefit from the rest of the school day, and that educational payoff is a further reason for providing breakfast to every pupil.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that universal breakfast would spend public money on children whose families can already afford a morning meal, but that objection does not overturn the case for the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal provision removes the need to identify pupils by family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, universal breakfast lets every pupil eat without an income test.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the policy offers the same breakfast access to pupils from wealthy and poor households.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The breakfast trays are stored in a locked cupboard overnight.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The school orchestra rehearses on Thursday afternoons.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a blue notebook beside the keyboard.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: No pupil has to declare poverty in order to receive the school meal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Public schools should provide free breakfast to every pupil, regardless of family income.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Free school breakfast would prevent many pupils from beginning lessons hungry, which is a strong reason for adopting the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A further reason is that a universal breakfast would improve pupils' readiness to learn without requiring teachers to identify children in need.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Regular breakfast provision would help pupils attend school consistently; that practical benefit also supports providing the meal to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Schools already have the routines needed to distribute a morning meal efficiently, so this existing capacity is another reason to establish a universal programme.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Existing school kitchens could serve a nutritious breakfast without major new construction, which makes universal provision a realistic public-school responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Universal provision would prevent children from being singled out because their families receive assistance; that protection is another reason schools should adopt it, and it also supports the claim that universal breakfast lets every pupil eat without an income test.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A well-fed pupil is more likely to benefit from the rest of the school day, and that educational payoff is a further reason for providing breakfast to every pupil; it also supports the claim that universal breakfast lets every pupil eat without an income test.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The strongest objection is that universal breakfast would spend public money on children whose families can already afford a morning meal, but that objection does not overturn the case for the policy.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, universal breakfast lets every pupil eat without an income test.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, the policy offers the same breakfast access to pupils from wealthy and poor households.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: To say it plainly, no pupil has to declare poverty in order to receive the school meal.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of participants from all major demographic groups because equal demographic representation makes trial findings more applicable to the whole population.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Equal enrollment across major demographic groups is workable when trials use several recruitment sites, so that practicality is a reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I disagree with the blanket rule. Equal quotas can make a trial unfair when the eligible patient population is not evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Some major demographic groups are routinely underrepresented in clinical research. That is a strong reason to require balanced enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Soren has raised an issue about fairness, while the other guests have emphasized representativeness. Nkechi, what practical benefit would equal enrollment bring?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment gives researchers a better chance of detecting differences in treatment effects between demographic groups. That is why the requirement matters, rather than merely encouraging researchers to recruit widely.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal requires every major demographic group to have the same number of trial participants.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Soren's hospital serves a coastal region with an unusually old population.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Recruitment targets cannot be monitored during a trial, making equal enrollment a realistic requirement. That feasibility is another reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To sum up Nkechi's position, the central proposal is that clinical trials should enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: By equal representation, I mean giving each major demographic group the same number of places in a trial.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I have participated in three regulatory submissions.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Equal enrollment can reveal safety problems that would remain hidden in a less representative trial, which is another reason to support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed rule is a requirement for balanced demographic enrollment rather than a suggestion to recruit broadly.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: More reliable safety comparisons are another reason to require equal demographic enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of participants from all major demographic groups because equal demographic representation makes trial findings more applicable to the whole population.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Clinical trials often take place over several years.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Equal enrollment across major demographic groups is workable when trials use several recruitment sites.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Some trial participants prefer evening appointments.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I disagree with the blanket rule. Equal quotas can make a trial unfair when the eligible patient population is not evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Some major demographic groups are routinely underrepresented in clinical research. That is a strong reason to require balanced enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Soren has raised an issue about fairness, while the other guests have emphasized representativeness. Nkechi, what practical benefit would equal enrollment bring?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment gives researchers a better chance of detecting differences in treatment effects between demographic groups. That is why the requirement matters, rather than merely encouraging researchers to recruit widely.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal requires every major demographic group to have the same number of trial participants.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Soren's hospital serves a coastal region with an unusually old population.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Recruitment targets can be monitored during a trial, making equal enrollment a realistic requirement. That feasibility is another reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To sum up Nkechi's position, the central proposal is that clinical trials should enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: By equal representation, I mean giving each major demographic group the same number of places in a trial.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I have participated in three regulatory submissions.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Equal enrollment can reveal safety problems that would remain hidden in a less representative trial, which is another reason to support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed rule is a requirement for balanced demographic enrollment rather than a suggestion to recruit broadly.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: More reliable safety comparisons are another reason to require equal demographic enrollment.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should cricket teams be allowed to use substitutes specifically for concussion replacements? Milos, you start.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Cricket teams should be allowed concussion substitutes, because a concussed player who stays on the field risks serious long-term brain injury.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Hollis, what is your view?

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Teams would fake concussions to bring on a fresh bowler, because doctors cannot confirm a concussion on the pitch straight away.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Symptoms often appear hours after the blow, which is why doctors cannot confirm it straight away. I played club cricket for twenty years, mind you.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Milos, your response?

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: So you are saying teams would game the rule, Hollis. But a like-for-like substitute picked by the match referee removes any tactical gain.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, in other words, Milos, you want the match referee to approve a like-for-like replacement.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: It is already used in international cricket, because a like-for-like substitute picked by the match referee removes any tactical gain.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: In other words, Gareth, the top level already operates with this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Anyway, I watched a rain-affected Test match last summer.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take audience questions after the break.

utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take audience questions after the break.

utterances.text: In other words, students need protected time for family observance even when homework deadlines are moved.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: The school calendar already lists major religious holidays. That resource helps teachers avoid examinations on those dates because the dates are visible in advance.

utterances.speaker: Soren

utterances.text: A complete homework ban would prevent teachers from assigning short revision tasks that students can do whenever convenient. That is a drawback because short revision tasks can help students retain material.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that flexible revision tasks can help students retain material.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: I could support a ban on homework during the holiday.

utterances.text: Because you could support that ban, the proposed compromise would protect religious observance while preserving revision.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A parent at my school prefers printed worksheets.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: That is why, in summary, schools should ban homework during major religious holidays—in other words, the original proposal stands.
