utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Schools should ban homework during major religious holidays. The reason is that homework assigned during those holidays increases pressure on students who are observing religious rituals.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: But a homework ban would make it harder for teachers to keep courses on schedule. That is because major religious holidays fall on different dates.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: So you are saying that a holiday homework ban would disrupt course schedules.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: My family observes one major religious holiday in the spring.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Students who complete assignments before a holiday often lose time needed for family observance.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Moving deadlines earlier merely puts the homework workload into the week before the holiday. For that reason, moving homework is not a satisfactory solution.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: In other words, students need protected time for family observance even when homework deadlines are moved.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: The school calendar already lists major religious holidays. That resource helps teachers avoid examinations on those dates because the dates are visible in advance.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Teachers receive advance warning of major religious holidays from the school calendar.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: A complete homework ban would prevent teachers from assigning short revision tasks that students can do whenever convenient. That is a drawback because short revision tasks can help students retain material.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Flexible revision tasks can help students retain material; this supports the earlier point about short revision tasks.

utterances.speaker: Bruno
utterances.text: Scheduling revision tasks after the holiday avoids interference with religious observance. That is why I could support a ban on homework during the holiday.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Because you could support that ban, the proposed compromise would protect religious observance while preserving revision.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: A parent at my school prefers printed worksheets.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: That is why, in summary, schools should ban homework during major religious holidays—in other words, the original proposal stands.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether apartment buildings should force residents to separate food waste from other rubbish. Joaquin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Yes, they should offer free food waste bins on every floor, because food waste is about a third of everything apartment residents throw away.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quick note first: the city council votes on a food waste proposal in March. Joaquin, anything more?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Separated scraps can also be composted into soil for city parks, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that kitchen scraps kept apart become free soil for the parks.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But a mandate is unenforceable in a block with a single shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Kai, what you mean is that nobody could police a shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: I back Joaquin, since food rotting in landfill releases methane, and another reason is that buildings which adopted food bins reported fewer rodent sightings.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Compliance in buildings with a mandate exceeds eighty percent, which shows it can work. I live on the ninth floor myself, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether apartment buildings should force residents to separate food waste from other rubbish. Joaquin, you start.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because food waste is about a third of everything apartment residents throw away.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quick note first: the city council votes on a food waste proposal in March. Joaquin, anything more?

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Separated scraps can also be composted into soil for city parks, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So you are saying that kitchen scraps kept apart become free soil for the parks.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But a mandate is unenforceable in a block with a single shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Kai, what you mean is that nobody could police a shared bin.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: I back Joaquin, since food rotting in landfill releases methane, and another reason is that buildings which adopted food bins reported fewer rodent sightings.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: Compliance in buildings with a mandate exceeds eighty percent, which shows it can work. I live on the ninth floor myself, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Mandates breed resentment among residents.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Small kitchens have no room for a second bin, so many residents of small flats will not comply.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I would rather see voluntary schemes, because the number of buildings with voluntary food bins has grown every year.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I prefer that route since voluntary composting costs little to start.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Fines would land on tenants who do not control the bins, which is another reason many will not comply, and a reason to keep things voluntary.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Put another way, buildings should encourage separation rather than force it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will have to leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Should local councils give tax discounts to shops that occupy vacant high-street premises? Camille, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Vacant high-street shops reduce pedestrian traffic for nearby businesses.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: That is why tax discounts could bring shops into vacant premises and restore pedestrian traffic.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Since bringing shops back would restore pedestrian traffic, local councils should offer tax discounts to shops that occupy vacant high-street premises.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Agnieszka, could such a scheme be administered without creating another costly bureaucracy?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The town's annual street festival is held in September.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: The council's tax office already has staff trained to process the proposed discount. Because the council's tax office already has staff trained to process the proposed discount, the administrative cost of the proposed discount would be low.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Camille, in other words, you are saying that tax discounts could bring shops into vacant premises and restore pedestrian traffic.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: One practical detail is that the council's retail committee meets on Thursdays.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: However, that proposal is too broad: local councils should not offer tax discounts to every shop that occupies a vacant high-street premise.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Welcome to tonight's debate. Should local councils give tax discounts to shops that occupy vacant high-street premises? Camille, why do you support the idea?

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Vacant high-street shops reduce pedestrian traffic for nearby businesses.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: That is why tax discounts could bring shops into vacant premises and restore pedestrian traffic.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: Since bringing shops back would restore pedestrian traffic, local councils should offer tax discounts to shops that occupy vacant high-street premises.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Agnieszka, could such a scheme be administered without creating another costly bureaucracy?

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: The town's annual street festival is held in September.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: The council's tax office can process the proposed discount with its existing software. Because the existing software can handle it, the administrative cost of the proposed discount would be low.

utterances.speaker: Milos
utterances.text: Camille, in other words, you are saying that tax discounts could bring shops into vacant premises and restore pedestrian traffic.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: However, that proposal is too broad: local councils should not offer tax discounts to every shop that occupies a vacant high-street premise.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference. That feature gives each ballot more information than a single mark.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice counting can transfer a voter's ballot to the next preferred candidate when the first choice is eliminated. This supports the proposition that ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Those transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority. This is a more demanding standard than merely receiving more votes than any individual rival.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a transferred ballot still expresses a voter's preference, a candidate who reaches a majority has support from more than half of participating voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That broader support gives the winner stronger democratic legitimacy. A majority-backed winner is easier to defend to constituents who preferred another candidate initially.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices would need to revise some ballot-counting software before adopting the system. That is a practical task, not a reason to preserve a weaker voting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Plurality voting is preferable because its ballots are simpler for voters to complete. A single mark is undeniably familiar.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that simplicity does not make plurality voting preferable when ranked-choice instructions can be learned quickly. The familiar method can still produce a winner without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear ballot instructions and a worked example allow voters to learn ranked-choice voting quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because voters can understand the procedure, a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. In other words, this is the same legitimacy advantage created by majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I would want election officials to publish counting procedures before the first ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting also reduces the risk that a spoiler candidate will distort the result. A candidate's presence need not force voters to abandon their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting makes it safer for voters to rank their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because spoiler pressure is reduced, sincere voting becomes more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For these reasons, ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference because a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. That feature gives each ballot more information than a single mark.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice ballots record fallback preferences, counting can transfer a voter's ballot to the next preferred candidate when the first choice is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Those transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority. This is a more demanding standard than merely receiving more votes than any individual rival.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a transferred ballot still expresses a voter's preference, a candidate who reaches a majority has support from more than half of participating voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That broader support gives the winner stronger democratic legitimacy. A majority-backed winner is easier to defend to constituents who preferred another candidate initially.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices would need to revise some ballot-counting software before adopting the system. That is a practical task, not a reason to preserve a weaker voting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Plurality voting is preferable because its ballots are simpler for voters to complete. A single mark is undeniably familiar.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that simplicity does not make plurality voting preferable when ranked-choice instructions can be learned quickly. The familiar method can still produce a winner without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear ballot instructions and a worked example allow voters to learn ranked-choice voting quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because voters can understand the procedure, a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has greater democratic legitimacy. In other words, this is the same legitimacy advantage created by majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting also reduces the risk that a spoiler candidate will distort the result. A candidate's presence need not force voters to abandon their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting makes it safer for voters to rank their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because spoiler pressure is reduced, sincere voting becomes more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For these reasons, ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.text: Those transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority. This is a more demanding standard than merely receiving more votes than any individual rival.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a transferred ballot still expresses a voter's preference, a candidate who reaches a majority has support from more than half of participating voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election administrators can publish a calendar for equipment maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. Constituents who preferred another candidate initially may find a majority-backed winner easier to defend.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices would need to revise some ballot-counting software before adopting the system. That is a practical task, not a reason to preserve a weaker voting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Plurality voting is preferable because its ballots are simpler for voters to complete. A single mark is undeniably familiar.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that simplicity does not make plurality voting preferable when ranked-choice instructions can be learned quickly. The familiar method can still produce a winner without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear ballot instructions and a worked example allow voters to learn ranked-choice voting quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because voters can understand the procedure, a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. In other words, this is the same legitimacy advantage created by majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I would want election officials to publish counting procedures before the first ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice voting reduces the risk that a spoiler candidate will distort the result, ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference. A candidate's presence need not force voters to abandon their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, ranked-choice voting makes it safer for voters to rank their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because spoiler pressure is reduced, sincere voting becomes more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For these reasons, ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections.

utterances.text: Yes, they should, because waiting rooms are not clogged with people who could have seen a pharmacist or a family doctor. A small fee would send them to the right place.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Jin, your view?

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: A charge would deter poorer patients with genuinely serious symptoms from coming in, since nobody can judge for themselves whether a chest pain or a child's fever is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: My own hospital ran a trial for six months.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Staff there redirected people to other services without charging them, and it worked.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: So, Jin, in other words, charging would make patients decide what counts as urgent, and they cannot do that reliably?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Many people only turn up at the emergency department because they cannot get a family doctor appointment. Attendance would fall if appointments were easier to get.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Sorry, my train home was delayed tonight, so I may need to wrap up soon.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: For background, emergency department fees already exist in some countries.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: That is to say, Amir, people who cannot get an appointment should not be fined for turning up at the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: Anders
utterances.text: A recent poll says voters like the idea of charging.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether marathon organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. Dimitri, make the case for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams give some runners access to drinks exactly when they want them. Because that unequal access helps those runners, it gives them a competitive advantage.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. The ban would create a more equal race because unequal access currently gives some runners an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: In other words, the fairness issue is unequal access to drinks. For context, the course has twelve official aid stations.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: No, personal hydration does not automatically give runners a competitive advantage. This is because many runners use personal hydration for convenience rather than to gain a competitive advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Because personal hydration does not automatically give runners a competitive advantage, a ban would force every runner to depend on official aid stations. That dependence would lengthen queues at those stations.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Those longer queues would make it harder for runners to maintain their pace.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: In other words, a ban would make race-day hydration less reliable.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Put another way, Leopold's position is that a ban would improve fairness, which is a reason to adopt it. The studio clock is running fast.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: A blanket ban would ignore runners who need to carry drinks for medical reasons. Some medical conditions require runners to carry drinks themselves, which is why the ban would be unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Organisers can require identical containers and limit handoffs to prevent personal hydration from creating an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Those safeguards can replace a blanket ban; that is why I reject the proposed ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The marathon route passes through three neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The race medals will be made from recycled metal.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether marathon organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. Dimitri, make the case for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams give some runners access to drinks exactly when they want them. Because that unequal access helps those runners, it gives them a competitive advantage.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. The ban would create a more equal race because unequal access currently gives some runners an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you are saying that the fairness issue is unequal access to drinks. For context, the course has twelve official aid stations.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: No, personal hydration does not automatically give runners a competitive advantage. Most runners use it because official aid stations become crowded, and that is why they carry their own drinks.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A ban would force every runner to depend on official aid stations. That dependence would lengthen queues at those stations.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Those longer queues would make it harder for runners to maintain their pace.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: In other words, a ban would make race-day hydration less reliable.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A ban would improve fairness, which is a reason to adopt it. The studio clock is running fast.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: A blanket ban would ignore runners who need to carry drinks for medical reasons. Some medical conditions require runners to carry drinks themselves, which is why the ban would be unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Organisers can require identical containers and limit handoffs to prevent personal hydration from creating an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Those safeguards can replace a blanket ban; that is why I reject the proposed ban.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether marathon organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. Dimitri, make the case for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams give some runners access to drinks exactly when they want them. Because that unequal access helps those runners, it gives them a competitive advantage.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. The ban would create a more equal race because unequal access currently gives some runners an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you are saying that the fairness issue is unequal access to drinks.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: No, personal hydration does not by itself give runners a competitive advantage. Most runners use it because official aid stations become crowded, and that is why they carry their own drinks.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A ban would force every runner to depend on official aid stations. That dependence would lengthen queues at those stations.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Those longer queues would make it harder for runners to maintain their pace.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: In other words, a ban would make race-day hydration less reliable.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Put another way, Leopold's position is that a ban would improve fairness, which is a reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: A blanket ban would ignore runners who need to carry drinks for medical reasons. Some medical conditions require runners to carry drinks themselves, which is why the ban would be unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Organisers can require identical containers and limit handoffs to prevent personal hydration from creating an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Those safeguards can replace a blanket ban; that is why I reject the proposed ban.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should councils stock free menstrual products in every public toilet?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes, councils should provide free menstrual products in all public toilets, because one in ten girls in our borough has missed school for lack of them.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: But councils that are already cutting budgets would find the cost too high.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: I would still say it should go ahead, since the scheme would cost only about 40p per resident per year. The council vote is next month, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the scheme costs next to nothing per head.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Yes. And it protects people's dignity, because nobody has to ask a stranger for help in an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Is there anything else in its favour?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: It also reduces the stigma around periods, which is another reason to say it protects dignity.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What about dispensers being damaged?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Vandalism has been rare in the pilot schemes, since the dispensers were checked every day.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, vandalism has not been a real problem with the dispensers.

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Right. Neighbouring councils should follow this lead, because our pilot cut missed school days by a third.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: Jelena
utterances.text: Only that I volunteered for years with a charity that hands out these products.

utterances.text: Governments should tax vacant homes where housing is short, since thousands of homes in tight markets sit empty all year.

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Then we write exemptions for renovation and probate into the tax.

utterances.speaker: Elif

utterances.speaker: Dalia
utterances.text: Rents here have risen faster than wages for ten years, remember.

utterances.text: Separately, vacancy rates in the city center were last surveyed three years ago.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether teachers should be allowed to grade class participation as part of final marks. Aurelio, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: I do. A participation grade can capture useful evidence about how students engage with learning.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Because participation grades capture engagement, teachers can notice questions and explanations that do not appear in written assignments.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Since that engagement is visible in discussion, students who explain ideas aloud can reveal misunderstandings before an exam.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Because participation is observed throughout the term, regular participation can encourage students to prepare for lessons.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Participation records can give teachers another way to recognize improvement; because of that, a participation grade can capture useful evidence about how students engage with learning.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: And because engagement includes responding to classmates, a participation mark can reward collaborative listening as well as frequent speaking.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The audience has been unusually quiet during this debate. Damien, you have argued that the system needs safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes. A detailed participation rubric can make classroom contributions easier to evaluate consistently.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: Because the rubric defines contribution, it can distinguish useful questions from attempts to attract attention.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since the criteria are written down, a rubric can allow teachers to record listening, teamwork and persistence.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Because students can see those criteria in advance, a rubric can tell students what kinds of contribution their teachers value.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: A published rubric also helps families, because it can give parents clearer information than a vague comment about attitude.

utterances.speaker: Arjun
utterances.text: And because schools can compare the same categories, a rubric can make participation marks easier to moderate across different classes.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: So the proposal is that teachers should be allowed to include class participation in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Exactly: teachers should be permitted to count classroom participation toward final marks.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: In other words, the debate concerns whether classroom engagement may form part of a student's final mark.

utterances.speaker: Aurelio
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed policy would allow participation to contribute to final grades.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: To summarize, teachers would be allowed to include participation in students' final marks.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But participation grades can penalize students who are shy, anxious or still learning the classroom language. That concern makes me oppose using them in final marks.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: The debate will end before the evening weather forecast. Our closing question is whether a careful rubric can answer Damien's objection.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should scientists be allowed to create embryos solely for laboratory research? Margit, you start.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because research on purpose-made embryos could show how to improve the success rate of IVF treatment.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Another reason is that leftover IVF embryos are too few, and often too poor in quality, for many studies.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: And the reason the research could reveal anything is that many miscarriages start in the first days of development, which only purpose-made embryos can show.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: But creating a human embryo only to destroy it treats that embryo as a mere tool.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: So you are saying, Ifeoma, that the embryo would be used as an object rather than respected?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: British law already caps embryo research at fourteen days.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: My sister had IVF treatment last year.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Some countries require that donors give consent before any embryo is used in research.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take audience questions after the break.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should scientists be allowed to create embryos solely for laboratory research? Margit, you start.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Yes, they should, because research on purpose-made embryos could reveal the causes of early miscarriage.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Another reason is that leftover IVF embryos are too few, and often too poor in quality, for many studies.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: And the reason the research could reveal anything is that miscarriage often begins in the earliest days of development, which only purpose-made embryos can show.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: But creating a human embryo only to destroy it treats that embryo as a mere tool.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: In other words, Ifeoma, you mean that the embryo would be used as an object rather than respected?

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: British law already caps embryo research at fourteen days.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: My sister had IVF treatment last year.

utterances.speaker: Eamon
utterances.text: Thank you all. We will take audience questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should senior managers spend a fixed proportion of their time mentoring junior employees? Zofia, you start.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Senior managers should spend a fixed share of their week mentoring juniors, because juniors who get regular guidance stay at the firm longer.

utterances.speaker: Cillian
utterances.text: They stay since guided juniors can see a career path here. I manage a logistics team of twelve, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: But a fixed quota turns mentoring into box-ticking.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying that a quota would reduce mentoring to a mere formality?

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: I back the fixed share, since explaining decisions to juniors sharpens a manager's own thinking. Our bank launched its scheme in 2019, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Birgit
utterances.text: Mentoring works best when it comes from a junior's own line manager.

utterances.speaker: Nadia
utterances.text: So you are saying that line managers, not senior managers, should do the mentoring. We will take questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should an independent commission, rather than legislators, draw electoral boundaries? Jasper, you start.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Legislators who draw the maps end up choosing their voters rather than the voters choosing them, since legislators should not draw their own boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But an unelected commission is the bigger danger to democracy, since commissioners can never be voted out.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Isaac, you have seen a commission at work.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Competitive seats in my state rose from four to eleven once the commission's maps took effect, so commissions deliver fairer contests.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: So you are saying commissions produce more competitive elections.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why legislators should not hold the pen. I should add that I chaired the commission's review panel.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Commissions are not above politics, since in many states the party leaders each nominate half of the members.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jasper, back to the legislators.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, a legislator who draws the map is judging his own re-election prospects.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So Camille, your worry is that nobody can ever remove a commissioner from office.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Exactly, whereas a legislature answers to voters for its maps, which is why a commission is the bigger danger. I started out as a redistricting clerk, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Maps drawn by legislators have been challenged in court in six states since 2010, so commissions would cut costly litigation, which is one more reason legislators should not draw the lines.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So you are saying commission-drawn maps end up in court less often.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Most states redraw their electoral boundaries once every ten years.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: But voters cannot punish a gerrymander when the map guarantees the seat.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: For the record, seven in ten legislative races are uncontested.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should an independent commission, rather than legislators, draw electoral boundaries? Jasper, you start.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Legislators should not draw their own boundaries, because they end up choosing their voters rather than the voters choosing them.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: But an unelected commission is the bigger danger to democracy, since commissioners can never be voted out.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Isaac, you have seen a commission at work.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Competitive seats in my state rose from four to eleven once the commission's maps took effect, so commissions deliver fairer contests.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: So you are saying commissions produce more competitive elections.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Yes, and that is why legislators should not hold the pen. I should add that I chaired the commission's review panel.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Commissions are not above politics, since in many states the party leaders each nominate half of the members.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jasper, back to the legislators.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Put another way, a legislator who draws the map is judging his own re-election prospects.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So Camille, your worry is that nobody can ever remove a commissioner from office.

utterances.speaker: Camille
utterances.text: Exactly, whereas a legislature answers to voters for its maps, which is why a commission is the bigger danger.

utterances.speaker: Valentina
utterances.text: Maps drawn by legislators have been challenged in court in six states since 2010, so commissions would cut costly litigation, which is one more reason legislators should not draw the lines.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So you are saying commission-drawn maps end up in court less often.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: But voters cannot punish a gerrymander when the map guarantees the seat, since seven in ten legislative races are uncontested.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.text: The agenda item is whether we should turn vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses. Petra, could you start with the building stock?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The municipality already owns several sound but vacant buildings. The municipality's building inventory includes photographs taken in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Sanna

utterances.speaker: Darius

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Sanna

utterances.speaker: Darius

utterances.speaker: Petra

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: The next council meeting is scheduled for Thursday evening.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Restaurants should not automatically add service charges to every bill. The reason is that an automatic charge removes the diner's ability to reward good service and withhold payment for bad service.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A guaranteed charge removes the incentive for staff to try hard, because staff who are paid the same whether or not diners are pleased have little reason to try.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many diners tip generously anyway, so a fixed charge adds nothing for them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Supporters say a mandatory charge makes pay fairer for kitchen and floor staff alike.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But a charge that is shared out by the restaurant can be fairer than tips, which favour those who work near the customers. It is only fair, though, if the restaurant discloses how it is divided.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once worked a summer as a dishwasher in a seaside cafe.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since diners often cannot tell whether a charge goes to staff or to the owner, the practice is murky.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Hidden charges breed distrust between customers and restaurants. In other words, customers feel cheated when a charge is printed in small type at the bottom of the bill.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Honest menu prices would make service charges unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Most diners would prefer to see one honest price up front, which is why that is the right route.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The Harbour Quarter has several restaurants that already print all-in prices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, restaurants should end the practice of automatic service charges and set honest menu prices instead.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: A personal annual training budget improves employee retention.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Tracking an individual training budget for every employee creates substantial administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Employees have different career goals and therefore need different kinds of training.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: The question is whether that difference justifies giving everyone a separate budget.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Adrian, should businesses be required to provide a personal annual training budget to every employee?

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Every business should be required to provide the same personal annual training budget to every employee.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi
utterances.text: Because a personal annual training budget improves retention, every business should give every employee one. Because every business should be required to provide the same personal annual training budget to every employee, a personal annual training budget would make employees more willing to stay with their employers.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Because tracking each employee's budget creates substantial administrative costs, a universal personal training budget would be impractical.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: Since employees have different career goals, businesses should let employees choose training that matches those goals.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: But small businesses have thin profit margins, so I cannot support a rigid requirement that applies to every employer.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Hiroshi, give us your response to the concern about a one-size-fits-all rule.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: In other words, your proposal is that every employee receive a personal annual training budget.

utterances.speaker: Giulia
utterances.text: To restate Adrian's concern, a personal training budget for everyone would create too much administrative work.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: So Giulia's point, put another way, is that training budgets should be tailored to employees' different career goals.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: Any training-budget policy should give small businesses flexibility over its size and administration. In other words, I am proposing flexibility for small businesses rather than one rigid budget rule.

utterances.speaker: Adrian
utterances.text: Because the administrative costs are substantial, businesses should use a shared catalogue of approved courses to reduce administration.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: For context, I have worked in human resources for twelve years.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: The debate is being broadcast from Studio Four.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Some employees attend evening courses.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: The panel has presented a case for individual budgets, but also a case for flexible implementation.

utterances.text: A personal annual training budget improves employee retention.

utterances.text: Tracking an individual training budget for every employee creates substantial administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: The question is whether that difference justifies giving everyone a separate budget.

utterances.speaker: Hiroshi

utterances.text: Since employees have different career goals, businesses should let employees choose training that matches those goals.

utterances.speaker: Deirdre
utterances.text: But small businesses have thin profit margins, so I cannot support a rigid requirement that applies to every employer.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Hiroshi, give us your response to the concern about a one-size-fits-all rule.

utterances.text: In other words, your proposal is that every employee receive a personal annual training budget.

utterances.speaker: Adrian

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether routine antibiotic use in livestock should be prohibited entirely. Hollis, you oppose a complete ban; why?

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: High-density livestock barns make disease outbreaks more likely.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Because those barns face that elevated risk, routine antibiotics can prevent some disease outbreaks in high-density livestock barns.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: Since routine antibiotics provide that preventive measure, a total prohibition would leave some livestock herds without antibiotics as their only practical preventive measure.

utterances.speaker: Jin
utterances.text: But vaccines can prevent many infections in livestock, which challenges the claim that antibiotics are the only practical option. Therefore, routine antibiotics are not essential in many livestock settings.

utterances.speaker: Carmen
utterances.text: So you are saying that routine antibiotics are not essential in many livestock settings. For that reason, routine antibiotic use should be prohibited entirely.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal is that routine antibiotic use should be prohibited entirely. Because of that prohibition, a total prohibition would reduce the spread of antibiotic resistance.

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: The debate is being recorded for the evening news.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: My family has kept goats for three generations.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the question of enforcement after the break.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: I think farmers should be banned from using certain pesticides within 200 metres of schools and playgrounds. The reason is that children's bodies absorb more chemical per kilo than adults' do.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: But spray drift beyond 200 metres is rare on calm days, so a blanket ban looks like overkill.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I farm right next to a primary school, and we already leave a buffer strip.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Which is another reason for the ban: a regional study found pesticide residues in the dust of classrooms near sprayed fields.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: I would back a legal rule, since voluntary buffers depend on each farmer's goodwill.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I oppose it, and the reason is that a ban would take about a tenth of small farms' land out of production.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying the ban would take about a tenth of small farms' land out of production?

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Yes. Unrelated, my daughter's school sports day is next week.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Compensation could cover the lost land, since the regional fund already pays farmers for keeping hedgerows.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: In other words, Josefa, the ban could be financed in just the same way as the hedgerow payments.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether schools should replace detention with restorative meetings after nonviolent misconduct. Fatima, make your case.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Schools should replace detention with restorative meetings after nonviolent misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: But detention is the only consequence pupils take seriously, because when my school dropped it, lateness rose by a fifth, and another reason is that detention teaches pupils nothing about the harm they caused.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: Fatima, how do restorative meetings do any better?

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: They make pupils face the person they wronged, so repeat offences fall, and that is another reason to drop detention.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: That makes sense, since pupils learn by facing the person they wronged.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, and repeat offences really do fall, because a district trial found them down by a third.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: So, Agnieszka, you are saying that without detention pupils stop taking rules seriously.

utterances.speaker: Agnieszka
utterances.text: Exactly. When my school dropped detention, lateness rose by a fifth, and you can trust that because I have run detentions for twenty years.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Detention is also unfair to pupils who must go home to care for siblings, because many pupils have caring duties at home.

utterances.speaker: Saanvi
utterances.text: In other words, Fatima, you want detention replaced by restorative meetings. We have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Hospitals should use AI to prioritise patients for scarce treatments, because a model can weigh far more clinical variables than a busy clinician can.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But models trained on past records would reproduce past bias against groups that were already under-treated.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The reason is that the training data encode systematic under-recording of some groups' symptoms, since women's pain, for one, has often been logged as milder than it was.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Which is another reason to support it: the ranking can be audited afterwards. That is because every input and weight is logged, while a clinician's reasoning is rarely written down. That logging is also the reason a model can weigh far more clinical variables than a busy clinician can, since every input it uses is recorded and a clinician's reasoning is rarely written down.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: So you are saying, Damien, that a prioritisation model would carry the old unfairness into its rankings?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I mean. For context, I am a nurse on a renal ward.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Put another way, Damien, the old blind spots in the data would become the model's blind spots.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Separately, my trust starts a trial of a scheduling tool next month.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Hospitals should not use AI to prioritise patients for scarce treatments, because a model can weigh far more clinical variables than a busy clinician can.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: But models trained on past records would reproduce past bias against groups that were already under-treated.

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: The reason is that the training data encode systematic under-recording of some groups' symptoms, since women's pain, for one, has often been logged as milder than it was.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Which is another reason for saying so: the ranking can be audited afterwards. That is because every input and weight is logged, while a clinician's reasoning is rarely written down.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: So you are saying, Damien, that a prioritisation model would carry the old unfairness into its rankings?

utterances.speaker: Damien
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I mean. For context, I am a nurse on a renal ward.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: Put another way, Damien, the old blind spots in the data would become the model's blind spots.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Separately, my trust starts a trial of a scheduling tool next month.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether health insurers should cover weight-loss medications for people who do not have diabetes. Gabriela, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Insurers should cover them, because obesity raises the risk of heart disease, joint failure and several cancers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Does the evidence show that the drugs work?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Trial results point the same way: patients lost roughly fifteen percent of their body weight, which is one more reason to cover them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Harriet, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Coverage would cost insurers far more than they would save, since the medications cost over a thousand dollars a month.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jolene?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Most patients regain the weight within a year of stopping the medication.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: That is why coverage would mean paying indefinitely, and so it supports Harriet's point on cost.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: My aunt was prescribed one of these last spring, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gabriela, how do you answer the cost point?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: But preventing a heart attack or a joint replacement saves insurers far more than the drug costs.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I see, so you are saying the avoided treatment would offset the price of the medications.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Still, diet and exercise programmes work for many patients and are far cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So where does that leave insurers?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quiet evening in the studio, I must say. Jolene, a last word.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So Harriet is saying insurers would be paying for these drugs indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Put another way, insurers should fund lifestyle programmes before medications.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Pregnant patients should receive paid time off for every antenatal appointment. The reason is that antenatal appointments are medically necessary rather than optional personal errands.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: I disagree. A universal paid-leave rule would impose significant costs on small employers, but that concern is not the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: My sister had her first antenatal appointment on a Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Paid time off protects pregnant patients from choosing between wages and medical care, which supports offering it for every appointment.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Our office has recently replaced its staff coffee machine.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A universal entitlement would reduce pressure on pregnant patients to postpone appointments. That is another reason to offer the time off.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Employers can plan for recurring antenatal appointment leave because antenatal appointments are usually scheduled in advance.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: Most antenatal appointments last less than two hours. That is an additional reason employers can plan for the leave.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: But predictable scheduling does not help patients whose appointments are changed at short notice.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: In other words, your point is that paid time off protects pregnant patients from having to choose between wages and medical care.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A statutory right to paid antenatal appointment leave can be administered fairly because employers could use a standard form that records appointment dates without requiring medical details.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A second reason that the right can be administered fairly is that the rule could require reasonable notice except when an appointment is urgent.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: A paid-leave entitlement would be workable with a simple employer record.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: So you are saying that the entitlement could be administered with a simple employer record.

utterances.speaker: Fiona
utterances.text: The proposal would cover routine check-ups as well as scans.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposal would cover both routine check-ups and scans.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Some antenatal clinics display posters about pregnancy nutrition.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Students who fail an exam may understand the material better when they retake it later. Because of that, I propose that students be permitted to retake failed exams without their original grades counting.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: I object to that proposal because removing the original grade would make a student's transcript less informative. Employers and graduate schools use transcripts to assess a student's initial performance.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: So you are saying that excluding the first grade would hide useful information about initial performance. Separately, the student services office closes at five o'clock on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: A second reason to support the policy is that a retake without grade penalty would let students demonstrate mastery after they have addressed their weaknesses. That would give students a fair opportunity to demonstrate later mastery.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: Students often improve after receiving detailed feedback on a failed exam, which is why retaking a failed exam can show genuine learning after feedback. That evidence of genuine learning after feedback supports your earlier claim that a retake without grade penalty would give students a fair opportunity to demonstrate later mastery.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, you consider a retake evidence of learning rather than merely a second score.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: I still oppose the proposal: removing original grades could widen inequality between students who can afford private coaching and students who cannot, because some students can afford extensive private coaching before a retake.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: Put another way, you think the proposed policy could reward students with greater financial resources.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: That evidence of genuine learning after feedback supports the claim that the proposed retake policy could be administered with the university's existing staff. In other words, it would not require the university to create a new administrative team.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The university has enough examination slots to schedule one retake period each term. Because the policy can be administered with existing staff and enough examination slots are available, the committee should approve retakes without the original grades counting.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: So the recommendation is to allow students one grade-neutral retake each term.

utterances.speaker: Helga
utterances.text: The next curriculum committee meeting is scheduled for Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should firms repay professional qualification fees only if staff stay on? Bilal, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Companies should repay fees only if the employee stays for a set period, because otherwise they end up training their competitors' workforce.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But that traps people in jobs they have outgrown. I paid for my own chartered exams last year, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a middle path in mind?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A clawback period is the fair compromise, since the firm gets a return and the employee still gets the qualification.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But it is coercive, because staff who cannot afford to repay the money are simply stuck.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Daniela, you are saying the clause amounts to forcing people to stay.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Firms need protection from losing their investment in training, which is why repayment should depend on staying.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, a retention period protects the training budget.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Clauses reduce turnover, since a study of regional banks found two-year clauses cut leavers by a third. That is another reason to back the compromise.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Daniela, your response?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Turnover is a symptom of poor management, so a clause treats the wrong problem.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That is why firms should pay fees upfront and raise wages instead.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: In other words, Daniela, you want the firm to carry the whole cost.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Fees can reach eleven thousand pounds a head.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: I should say that I work for a professional training provider.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. A lively exchange.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should firms repay professional qualification fees only if staff stay on? Bilal, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Companies should repay fees only if the employee stays for a set period, because otherwise they end up training their competitors' workforce.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But that traps people in jobs they have outgrown. I paid for my own chartered exams last year, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a middle path in mind?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A clawback period is the fair compromise, since the firm gets a return and the employee still gets the qualification.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But a clawback clause is coercive, which is why staff who cannot afford to repay the money are simply stuck.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Daniela, you are saying the clause amounts to forcing people to stay.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Fees can reach eleven thousand pounds a head, so firms need protection from losing that money, which is why repayment should depend on staying.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, a retention period protects the training budget.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Clauses reduce turnover, since a study of regional banks found two-year clauses cut leavers by a third. That is another reason to back the compromise.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Daniela, your response?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Turnover is a symptom of poor management, so a clause treats the wrong problem.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That is why firms should pay fees upfront and raise wages instead.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: In other words, Daniela, you want the firm to carry the whole cost.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: I should say that I work for a professional training provider.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Separately, many employers already offer paid study leave for exam preparation.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Qualification fees also differ widely between professions.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. A lively exchange.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should firms repay professional qualification fees only if staff stay on? Bilal, start us off.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Companies should repay fees only if the employee stays for a set period, because otherwise they end up training their competitors' workforce.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But that traps people in jobs they have outgrown. I paid for my own chartered exams last year, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Lars, you have a middle path in mind?

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: A clawback period is the fair compromise, since the firm gets a return and the employee still gets the qualification.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: But it is coercive, because staff who cannot afford to repay the money are simply stuck.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Daniela, you are saying the clause amounts to forcing people to stay.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: Fees can reach eleven thousand pounds a head, so firms need protection from losing that money, which is why repayment should depend on staying.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Put another way, a retention period protects the training budget.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: Clauses make staff far less likely to leave, since a study of regional banks found two-year clauses cut leavers by a third. That is another reason to back the compromise.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Daniela, your response?

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: Turnover is a symptom of poor management, so a clause treats the wrong problem.

utterances.speaker: Daniela
utterances.text: That is why firms should pay fees upfront and raise wages instead.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: In other words, Daniela, you want the firm to carry the whole cost.

utterances.speaker: Lars
utterances.text: I should say that I work for a professional training provider.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. A lively exchange.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Creators should be required to watermark realistic synthetic videos, because viewers cannot reliably tell them from genuine footage by eye.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Fabricated clips of public figures can spread widely before anyone corrects them, which is a second reason for the rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A mark would let platforms and viewers identify synthetic videos quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Admittedly, watermarks are easy to crop or strip out, so a requirement would not stop determined deceivers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But most deceptive clips that circulate come from casual uploaders who do not bother to remove marks, which ignores nothing in that objection yet blunts it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The earlier point about stripping out marks stands, since a watermark rule would not work against the most determined deceivers.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once watched a fake news clip fool an entire family dinner.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a watermark requirement works as a label that tells viewers what they are watching.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Honest creators lose little by adding a small mark to their work, and that is one more reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Watermark standards differ between countries.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Synthetic videos are becoming more realistic every year.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether low-income defendants should receive free legal representation in all civil eviction cases. Jasper, why do you support that policy?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Low-income defendants often cannot afford a lawyer. For that reason, they should receive free legal representation in every civil eviction case.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: I disagree with that approach. Providing free representation in every civil eviction case would lengthen hearings and increase court costs, but universal free legal representation is too broad.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Represented defendants are more likely to understand the filing deadlines in eviction proceedings, which is one reason the policy deserves support.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Legal representation can prevent avoidable evictions caused by procedural mistakes. That is another reason to guarantee it in every civil eviction case.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Femi, do you think the policy would create benefits as well as costs?

utterances.speaker: Beatriz

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: I say this partly because my sister did not go through IVF last year.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: But only wealthy families could afford this kind of selection, and that cuts against allowing it freely.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: That is to say, the technology would be there for the rich and not for the poor.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: UK regulators currently license embryo screening clinic by clinic.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Put another way, the choice should be legal for parents.

utterances.text: Public opinion polls show that people are divided on genetic selection of embryos.

utterances.text: A specialist vacancy can take months to fill; because of that, small employers struggle to cover an employee's absence during a sabbatical.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying that a specialist vacancy may remain unfilled for months.

utterances.speaker: Bongani

utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether employees should be allowed to take paid sabbaticals after five years of service. Bongani, make the case for the policy.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are saying that a specialist vacancy may remain unfilled for months.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: A company survey found that 68 percent of employees acquired new digital skills during paid sabbaticals. That evidence supports the earlier claim that employees who take paid sabbaticals often return with updated skills, and it is also why I support the five-year rule.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: The company's cafeteria closes at six o'clock.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments build desalination plants despite their high energy use and their marine impacts? Wilhelmina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Governments should build them, because rainfall in coastal cities is simply no longer reliable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: But the plants consume enormous amounts of electricity, and that is what your case ignores. I live a short walk from the one at the harbour, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Wilhelmina, how do you answer on the rainfall point?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Rainfall really is unreliable, since reservoir levels in the region have fallen by a third in a decade.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: The energy bill is just as real, because each cubic metre of desalinated water needs about three kilowatt-hours.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tariq, what about the sea itself?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Brine discharge raises salinity right around the outfalls, which is why seagrass and fish nearby get damaged.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Tariq, you are saying that brine from these plants does serious damage to marine ecosystems.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Governments should build them, which is why the marine impact can be kept small, because modern diffusers dilute brine to ambient salinity within a few dozen metres.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So you are saying the harm to marine life is minor. My brother works at a plant in the Gulf, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: Put another way, these plants are among the biggest electricity users in the whole water sector.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, the region's rain-fed supply is draining away, which Gareth's point that these plants are among the biggest electricity users in the water sector shows, and that is what we have to plan for.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments build desalination plants despite their high energy use and their marine impacts? Wilhelmina, you start.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Governments should build them, because rainfall in coastal cities is simply no longer reliable.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gareth, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: But the plants consume enormous amounts of electricity, and that is what your case ignores. I live a short walk from the one at the harbour, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Wilhelmina, how do you answer on the rainfall point?

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: Rainfall really is unreliable, since reservoir inflows in the region have halved over the past thirty years.

utterances.speaker: Gareth
utterances.text: The energy bill is just as real, because each cubic metre of desalinated water needs about three kilowatt-hours.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tariq, what about the sea itself?

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: Brine discharge raises salinity right around the outfalls, which is why seagrass and fish nearby get damaged.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Tariq, you are saying that brine from these plants does serious damage to marine ecosystems.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: The marine impact can be kept small.

utterances.speaker: Tariq
utterances.text: So you are saying the harm to marine life is minor. My brother works at a plant in the Gulf, for what it is worth.

utterances.speaker: Wilhelmina
utterances.text: In other words, the region's rain-fed supply is draining away, and that is what we have to plan for.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land? Ifeoma, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Councils should ban them, because petrol blowers are far louder than electric ones.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kieran, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: I do. A ban would leave parks departments unable to clear wet leaves from big sites, since battery blowers run out within forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Petrol blowers also throw out huge amounts of fine particulates, which is another reason to ban them.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: And that is a reason too: the workers who operate them breathe the exhaust all day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Sunita, the reason operators breathe the exhaust all day is that operators are being harmed by the exhaust of their own machines.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A ban would hit council budgets, because battery blowers cost three times as much as petrol ones.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: But the extra cost would be small, since councils already buy electric hedge trimmers in bulk at a discount.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Kieran, is that a ban would leave grounds crews without working equipment for big jobs.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: That is it.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Residents' noise complaints about leaf blowers doubled last year, which shows a ban would be welcome.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: The council's grounds depot is next to the old station, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.
