utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land? Ifeoma, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Councils should ban them, because petrol blowers are far louder than electric ones.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kieran, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: I do. A ban would leave parks departments unable to clear wet leaves from big sites, since battery blowers run out within forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Petrol blowers also throw out huge amounts of fine particulates, which is another reason to ban them.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: And that is a reason too: the workers who operate them breathe the exhaust all day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Sunita, operators are being harmed by the exhaust of their own machines.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A ban would force councils to cut spending on other services.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: But the extra cost would be small, since councils already buy electric hedge trimmers in bulk at a discount.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Kieran, is that a ban would leave grounds crews without working equipment for big jobs.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: That is it. For the record, I ran a council grounds team for ten years. Battery blowers cost three times as much as petrol ones, incidentally.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Residents' noise complaints about leaf blowers doubled last year, which shows a ban would be welcome.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: The council's grounds depot is next to the old station, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land? Ifeoma, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Councils should ban them, because petrol blowers are far louder than electric ones.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kieran, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: I do. A ban would leave parks departments unable to clear wet leaves from big sites, since battery blowers run out within forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Petrol blowers also throw out huge amounts of fine particulates, which is another reason to ban them.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: And that is a reason too: the workers who operate them breathe the exhaust all day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Sunita, operators are being harmed by the exhaust of their own machines.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A ban would hit council budgets, because battery blowers cost three times as much as petrol ones.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: But the extra cost would be small, since councils already buy electric hedge trimmers in bulk at a discount.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: So what you are saying, Kieran, is that a ban would leave grounds crews without working equipment for big jobs.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: That is it. For the record, I ran a council grounds team for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Residents' noise complaints about leaf blowers doubled last year, which shows a ban would be welcome.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: The council's grounds depot is next to the old station, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: That is all we have time for. Thanks to you all.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether supermarkets should be banned from selling below wholesale cost. Anika, you start.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Supermarkets should be prohibited from selling below wholesale cost.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: But below-cost selling keeps food cheap for families on tight budgets.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: For the record, milk is the product most often sold at a loss.

utterances.speaker: Anika
utterances.text: Some small grocers can match a price below wholesale cost, since below-cost selling drives small grocers out of business.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: So, in other words, Anika, you are saying below-cost selling kills off corner shops.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Put another way, Efua, what you mean is that families on tight budgets would pay more if it were banned.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Yes. I should add that I shop at a corner shop myself on Sundays.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether blood donors should receive small financial payments. Naveen, please make the case.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: I propose that the committee offer blood donors small financial payments because blood-donor registrations have fallen this year.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: I am concerned, but small financial payments could reduce donations from people motivated by altruism.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: What benefits would the payment scheme provide?

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: Another reason to offer the payments is that they could attract occasional donors who do not currently donate.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So you are proposing that the committee pay blood donors small amounts of money?

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: Before we continue, the meeting room's projector has been unreliable this month.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: In other words, Clement's objection is that payments could reduce donations motivated by altruism. Since offering small payments is the proposal before us, I recommend a six-month pilot.

utterances.speaker: Naveen
utterances.text: A further reason to run the pilot is that comparing paid and unpaid recruitment drives would cost less than a national recruitment campaign.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: The finance question is manageable. Since the committee should run a six-month pilot offering small payments to blood donors, a six-month payment pilot could be audited for its effects on donor numbers and motivation.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: We will record the pilot recommendation for a vote.

utterances.speaker: Clement
utterances.text: The finance subcommittee meets next Friday.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: I think councils should swap some on-street parking for secure bike storage, because one car space holds about ten bikes in a locked cage.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: That is a reason I would add to, since plenty of terraced-street residents never cycle because they have nowhere safe to keep a bike.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: But taking spaces away would hurt the shops that rely on customers arriving by car.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: That ignores the retail studies of pedestrianised streets, which often find takings stay level or rise.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying, Efua, that removing parking would damage shops.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Funny thing, my own corner shop is on a street with no parking at all.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Bike theft is the main reason people give for not cycling here, which means secure storage tackles exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I would start with a small trial of storage in a few streets.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, you think a small trial is the sensible first step.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Unrelated, but the bus I take home is always late on Fridays.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Disabled drivers need nearby kerbside spaces, so no removal should touch the bays reserved for them.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Replacing parking with storage need not touch disabled bays.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Lorenzo, put another way, storage can replace ordinary spaces while keeping disabled bays.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Then I could accept it as long as only ordinary spaces go.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Job applicants should be informed of the salary before they submit an application. Salary disclosure gives employers more focused applications from people who accept the stated pay range, and that is why the policy is worth adopting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because the salary is visible at the outset, applicants can decide whether a job is worth pursuing before they spend time applying.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That benefit has a limitation: early salary disclosure may narrow the applicant pool. This possible reduction is an objection to requiring disclosure, but it does not outweigh the time saved by applicants.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Employers can nevertheless gain more focused applications, because people who reject the stated pay range will leave before applying.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, applicants can screen out jobs whose stated pay does not suit them before applying. Because this screening happens early, it produces the more focused applications described above.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, employers should publish the salary before accepting applications.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many job seekers revise their résumés several times before sending them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear job descriptions also help applicants understand what work a position involves.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Job applicants should be told the salary before they submit an application. Salary disclosure can reduce the number of unsuitable applications employers must review, and that is why the policy is worth adopting.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because the salary is visible at the outset, applicants can decide whether a job is worth pursuing before they spend time applying.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That benefit has a limitation: early salary disclosure may narrow the applicant pool. This possible reduction is an objection to requiring disclosure, but it does not outweigh the time saved by applicants.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Employers can nevertheless gain more focused applications, because people who reject the stated pay range will leave before applying.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, applicants can screen out jobs whose stated pay does not suit them before applying. Because this screening happens early, it produces the more focused applications described above.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, employers should publish the salary before accepting applications.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Many job seekers revise their résumés several times before sending them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Clear job descriptions also help applicants understand what work a position involves.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets. Noor, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: New housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets because trees reduce summer heat around them.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I grew up on a treeless housing estate, so I understand why people want greenery nearby.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, Noor is arguing that mandatory canopy rules are justified by their cooling benefits.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The city lost more than two hundred mature trees during housing construction last year. That is why the city should prevent housing construction from causing further tree loss.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Padraig, what is the strongest objection to a fixed target?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Planting trees during construction is cheaper than retrofitting them later, so developers can meet a tree-canopy target without major redesigns.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: The difficulty is that mandatory canopy targets can raise rents in smaller housing developments; for that reason, mandatory canopy targets should not apply to every housing development.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that affordability concerns outweigh protection from summer heat.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: No, mandatory canopy targets need not raise rents when developments retain existing trees. Developers can retain mature trees during construction, which is why this alternative deserves attention.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Can the rule be adjusted rather than abandoned?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Phased canopy targets let builders preserve existing trees.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Put another way, phased canopy targets allow builders to preserve existing trees while meeting the tree-canopy requirement.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Because developers can retain mature trees during construction, the city should publish canopy maps before approving housing projects. Regarding those maps, they would identify areas where the city should require stronger canopy targets because they have little existing tree cover.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: My neighborhood association is holding its annual meeting next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: To sum up Malik's recommendation, he wants the city to require stronger canopy targets in areas with little existing tree cover.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets. Noor, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: New housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets because trees reduce summer heat around them.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I grew up on a treeless housing estate, so I understand why people want greenery nearby.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, Noor is arguing that mandatory canopy rules are justified by their cooling benefits.

utterances.text: The annual meeting of my neighborhood association is next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: To sum up Malik's recommendation, he wants the city to require stronger canopy targets in areas with little existing tree cover.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Item two: fixed allowance or pay for completed chores. Sunita, would you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: I favour a fixed weekly allowance, because it teaches children to budget.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Budgeting needs a predictable income, which is why a fixed amount is what teaches it.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I disagree with a flat allowance, though: paying per chore teaches children that money is earned through effort, and a flat sum never does.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: So you are saying that paying per chore ties a child's money to their effort.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew starts school next week.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Children paid per chore will refuse any unpaid task, since they will ask what they get for every job.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: That is why parents should not pay children for chores, which is one more reason for a flat allowance.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: So what you mean is that chores should stay unpaid family duties.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I would pay a small fixed allowance plus paid extras, since the base teaches budgeting and the extras teach that money is earned.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Paid extras would also cost a family little, which is another reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Ulla's plan of a small fixed allowance plus paid extras is sound, because a fixed base combined with paid bonus jobs is the right system.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: We should schedule next month's review before the school holidays.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Item two: fixed allowance or pay for completed chores. Sunita, would you start us off?

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: I favour a fixed weekly allowance, because it teaches children to budget.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Budgeting needs a predictable income, which is why a fixed amount is what teaches it.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I disagree with a flat allowance, though: paying per chore teaches children that money is earned through effort, and a flat sum never does.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: So you are saying that paying per chore ties a child's money to their effort.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: By the way, my nephew starts school next week.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: Children paid per chore will refuse any unpaid task, since they will ask what they get for every job.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: That is why parents should not pay children for chores, which is one more reason for a flat allowance.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I agree with that, because chores should stay unpaid family duties.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: I would pay a small fixed allowance plus paid extras, since the base teaches budgeting and the extras teach that money is earned.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Paid extras would also cost a family little, which is another reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: In other words, a fixed base combined with paid bonus jobs is the right system.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: We should schedule next month's review before the school holidays.

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should annual bonuses depend more on team performance than on individual targets? Laleh, make the case for changing the balance.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team performance reveals whether colleagues share responsibility for results.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Individual targets can leave important teamwork unmeasured.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Because team performance reveals shared responsibility, bonuses should give team results a larger weight.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Since individual targets can leave important teamwork unmeasured, employers should reduce the weight of individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: That evidence is why a substantial team-based bonus component would improve cooperation.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: For that reason, firms should review individual targets before paying bonuses.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Team-based bonuses would make employees discuss dependencies earlier, because team performance reveals whether colleagues share responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Because individual targets can leave important teamwork unmeasured, team performance measures can reveal free-riding that individual targets miss.

utterances.speaker: Laleh
utterances.text: Since team performance reveals shared responsibility, annual bonuses should depend more on team results than on individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: So you are saying that giving team results a larger weight is the proposed change to the bonus system.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: In other words, Femi's recommendation is to reduce the weight of individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Put another way, team performance measures can expose free-riding that individual targets miss. However, that is an objection to letting team results outweigh individual targets.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: We will return after the break for closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Tonight we are discussing whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Annelise, you support the change.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Twice-yearly conferences let teachers discuss a student's progress in detail, which is why the replacement is worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My daughter has attended the same school since kindergarten. I am not convinced that a meeting can replace something families can read at home.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: The new system would give families specific next steps, because a conversation can turn preparation into an actionable plan.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Those specific next steps would make it easier for families to support learning between meetings. That is why conferences could lead to more useful follow-up than a report card alone.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Maeve, what is your strongest objection to replacing the reports?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later. Because that record remains available after a meeting, schools should retain a written reporting system alongside any conferences.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So Annelise is proposing that schools use two parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards. Maeve, do you think the written record is essential?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, Maeve is saying that report cards offer parents a lasting written record. We will leave the audience to weigh that concern against the proposed follow-up benefits.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes, I support that requirement. Because I support that requirement, a minority juror can identify overlooked evidence or reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: You have thought about the issue carefully. What makes unanimity important?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I have never served on a jury.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I also prefer written questions to live interview questions.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Unanimous verdicts make jurors take reasonable doubt seriously; because of that, I support that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest objection to your position?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But a single juror can block a verdict despite very strong evidence. That danger is why serious criminal trials should allow a retrial after a jury deadlock.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying that a deadlock should lead to a retrial rather than an immediate conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Exactly. A single dissent can force a serious criminal trial to be repeated, and because of that every serious-offence trial needs a clear procedure for dealing with a deadlocked jury.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, you think unanimous verdicts need a defined deadlock procedure.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Yes. Several comparable legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts; this comparison shows that unanimity is not the only possible way to protect fairness in serious criminal trials.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Your comparative point is that qualified-majority systems provide an alternative to unanimous verdicts, and that point supports the claim that unanimity is not the only possible way to protect fairness in serious criminal trials.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Before we finish, is there anything personal you want to add?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I keep a copy of the jury handbook on my desk.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Managers should be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Internal candidates already understand the organisation's processes, which is one reason for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that are missing inside the organisation. However, internal advertising can create a costly delay in filling a position.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: A prolonged vacancy can overload the existing team; that is why the delay is costly.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, you think internal advertising can create a costly delay in filling a position.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Managers can set a five-day window for internal applications. Because that window is short, it need not create a long hiring delay.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal advertising makes the promotion process more transparent.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Employees trust promotion decisions more when opportunities are visible, so transparency has a practical benefit.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that visible opportunities make employees more trusting of promotion decisions.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: Internal advertising gives employees a fair chance to apply, which is another reason managers should follow the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Put another way, managers should be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: As a side note, I usually take the tram to work on Fridays. That policy gives employees a fair opportunity to apply before external recruitment begins.

utterances.speaker: Matteo
utterances.text: The organisation's recruitment policy was last reviewed in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should governments cap the fees that payment processors charge small businesses? Pradeep, you start.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Governments should cap those fees, because processors take around three percent of every card sale from small shops, which eats a large share of their thin margins.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Pradeep, that holds because processing fees swallow much of a small shop's profit.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: But a cap would push processors to stop serving small businesses, since fraud losses on small merchants are higher than on large chains.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: That is because small merchants rarely have fraud-screening tools.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Olumide, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: I support a cap, since large retailers negotiate much lower rates than corner shops.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: In other words, the corner shop ends up subsidising the big chain.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: Card terminals are now installed even in very small shops.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: I favour promoting competition among processors.

utterances.speaker: Olumide
utterances.text: So you are saying, Petra, that a cap would shut small shops out of card payments. By the way, my sister owns a bakery in Lagos.

utterances.speaker: Pradeep
utterances.text: Small businesses deserve special protection from the market power of processors, because they make up most of the merchants accepting cards.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Separately, open-banking payments are already cheaper than card payments.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are nearly out of time. For the record, our studio audience was polled on this question last week.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Some countries publish the average fees processors charge businesses.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should youth football leagues prohibit heading until players reach sixteen? Dolores, you support the motion.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen because repeated heading can cause cumulative effects from minor impacts.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A blanket prohibition on heading is unnecessary because trained coaches can teach safe heading technique without allowing heading in matches.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Players under sixteen need gradual preparation before they can head the ball safely, and gradual preparation can be provided through soft balls and controlled drills.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: A complete ban would prevent coaches from identifying players who need extra help with heading technique, since regular supervised practice helps coaches identify those players.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Karima, does your alternative allow any heading in competitive matches?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: The regional youth league introduced new concussion forms this season. That administrative change does not settle the question before us.

utterances.speaker: Florin

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether schools should abolish class rankings to reduce unhealthy competition among students.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: The district has eighteen secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Amir, what policy would you put to the schools?

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Schools should abolish class rankings. The question is whether competition is helping students learn.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: The reason I support abolition is that class rankings cause students to concentrate on their standing instead of their learning. Abolishing them would also let teachers emphasize individual improvement.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I disagree with abolishing rankings altogether, because class rankings provide students with useful feedback about their performance.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: Public rank lists make students compare social status. Because students then compare status instead of progress, comparing social status increases anxiety among students; that is why schools should abolish class rankings.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Because Amir is saying that schools should abolish class rankings, schools should adopt that policy.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: I was ranked fourth in my graduating class, and that experience shaped how I think about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Rohan
utterances.text: Schools should retain private progress reports because private progress reports identify the subjects in which each student needs help.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: We will now hear another comment.

utterances.speaker: Leilani
utterances.text: Private progress reports give useful feedback without creating a public ladder of status.

utterances.speaker: Amara
utterances.text: In other words, schools should keep feedback private rather than publish a ranking.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: One more reason to abolish rankings is that doing so would allow schools to recognize cooperation instead of competition.

utterances.speaker: Amir
utterances.text: Because schools should use private progress reports as their feedback system, schools should retain them.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Our question is whether councils should let residents decide directly how a fixed share of the annual budget is spent. Dolores, you support the idea.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: A fixed portion of the annual budget would limit the scope of residents' decisions; because of that safeguard, councils should let residents vote directly on how that portion is spent.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: For that same reason, a limited vote would give residents meaningful influence without handing them control of the whole budget.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Gabriela, what protects essential services under this arrangement?

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Essential services need protection from year-to-year budget swings.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Because essential services need that protection, a fixed budget cap would keep resident votes from diverting funds away from essential services. The cap would also make annual financial planning more predictable, for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Residents are more likely to participate when they can see a direct connection between their choices and local results.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: That is why direct budget votes would increase civic participation.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: One practical point is that councils can offer voting both online and in public libraries, so direct budget ballots can reach residents who cannot attend council meetings.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: But an organised minority could capture a fixed-portion budget vote; that is an objection to allowing residents to decide the spending.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: So you are saying that a limited budget vote would give residents influence without giving them control of the whole budget.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: To put Dolores's point another way, the cap would stop resident votes from taking money away from essential services.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: In other words, Dolores believes the cap would make yearly council budgeting more predictable.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: As an aside, my neighbourhood opened a new pedestrian footbridge this year.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: I have not decided how I would vote on the proposal.

utterances.text: So you are saying cursive is a poor use of limited lesson time.

utterances.text: Handwritten exams remain the norm in secondary school, which means pupils who cannot write fluently by hand will be penalised.

utterances.speaker: Tobias
utterances.text: What you mean is that pupils need handwriting in order to cope with exams.

utterances.speaker: Bilal
utterances.text: For the record, my son's class types forty words a minute by age nine.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is all we have time for tonight.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: We are considering whether gene editing should be permitted to prevent inherited diseases in human embryos. A licensing system could monitor gene editing in human embryos.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, a licensing system could monitor gene editing in human embryos. Because monitored editing could be controlled, it could prevent some severe inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: That monitoring capacity is also why permitting embryo gene editing under licensing would give families a regulated way to avoid some severe inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Strict rules would be needed before embryo gene editing could be permitted.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Because strict rules are necessary, they should limit editing to serious inherited diseases. The same rules should require independent review of every proposed treatment.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Independent review would make decisions about embryo editing more accountable.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Because accountable decisions would improve oversight, public oversight of embryo editing would become more credible. Accountable decisions would also make it easier to identify unsafe editing experiments.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: Embryo gene editing should be permitted only after long-term safety evidence is available.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Since long-term safety evidence is essential, it should be a condition of permitting embryo gene editing.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Because strict rules would be needed before embryo gene editing could be permitted, the committee's draft policy allows embryo gene editing only for serious inherited diseases.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: In other words, the committee's draft policy excludes editing for cosmetic enhancement.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The proposed review process would include geneticists, clinicians and patient representatives.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: Put another way, the proposed review process would not be controlled by geneticists alone.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: Some embryo-editing laboratories operate in coastal cities.

utterances.speaker: Efua
utterances.text: The meeting room's ventilation system was repaired last month.

utterances.speaker: Orla
utterances.text: The committee received twelve written submissions before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: Zofia
utterances.text: However, a licensing system could not reliably detect every unsafe embryo-editing experiment.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether governments should force every electric car onto one charging standard. Josefa, you start.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Governments should require one universal standard, because drivers can't currently be sure a public charger will fit their car.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: But a mandate would freeze the technology in place, since better connectors are still being developed.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Drivers can't be sure because three different plug types are in common use on public networks.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Theo, you run charging stations. What do you see?

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Fitting several plug types at every site raises our installation costs.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So, Theo, you are saying that supporting several plug types makes stations more expensive to build.

utterances.speaker: Theo
utterances.text: Exactly. A single standard would lower prices for drivers, because stations would need to fit only one connector.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I'll put my point another way: a mandate would lock in today's connector for fifteen years or more.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying today's connector would be fixed for fifteen years or more.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Yes, and charging speeds have doubled in five years, which shows connectors are still improving. I should add that I only charge at home myself.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Thank you all. That is the end of tonight's debate.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Item two: whether the government should pay towards satellite internet for homes with no reliable broadband. Seamus, you start.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I say yes, we should subsidise it, because laying fibre to remote farms would cost far more per household than a satellite subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Satellite is only a stopgap, and it locks households into a private provider.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: My cousin runs a sheep farm and still uses a dial-up line.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: That is why I say the subsidy would simply hand public money to one company, since a stopgap that locks people in benefits only the provider.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: But the money would go to households, not the company, and they could spend it on any approved provider.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: So you are saying it works like a voucher that households can use anywhere approved.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Sorry, the projector has been flickering all morning, can someone look at it?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Also, rural children without reliable internet fall behind in schoolwork that is set online, which is a reason to act.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: In other words, with online homework a home connection is essential for pupils.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Then let us do a pilot subsidy in two rural districts for a year.

utterances.speaker: Josefa
utterances.text: Separately, satellite dishes need a clear view of the sky to work properly.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: That is to say, a small trial before we commit to a national scheme.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Yes, terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because adults have authority over decisions about their own bodies.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Palliative care cannot relieve every kind of suffering, which is why the right matters. The reason is that pain stays uncontrolled for some patients even in the best hospices.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Critics object, though, that vulnerable people could be pressured into choosing death.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: That ignores the screening: it would detect most pressure on vulnerable patients, because a request would need approval from two doctors and a waiting period.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Oregon has run its law since 1997 without evidence of widespread abuse, which shows that the screening works.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: I volunteered in a hospice for three years.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: No doctor would be obliged to take part. In other words, doctors could opt out.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: The right should exist since anyone who dislikes the idea never has to ask for it. Put another way, it is an option, not an obligation.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Waiting periods help the screening work, because they give patients time to reconsider; that time matters since a patient can withdraw a request at any point.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: To put it differently, approval would be slow and double-checked. That is to say, dying people would still have a say in how their lives end.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: My grandmother died in 2015.

utterances.speaker: Fatima
utterances.text: Assisted dying laws also differ in which diagnoses they cover from one country to another.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. Ayesha, please begin.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Merging neighbouring refuse-collection services would reduce administrative costs. The councils currently maintain separate billing, procurement, and management offices, so combining them would remove duplicated work.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: I have worked on a municipal waste committee, but I am not convinced that a merger is automatically wise.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: Some households put out extra garden waste after storms. That seasonal problem deserves attention even if the authorities keep their services separate.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Neighbouring councils already use compatible route-planning software. Because the software is compatible, a merged service could coordinate its depots.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Coordinated depots would reduce empty journeys by refuse vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Felix
utterances.text: But merging the services could make a failure at one depot disrupt collections across both councils. That risk is a serious objection to the cost-saving case.

utterances.speaker: Sipho
utterances.text: To put Felix's concern another way, a single depot failure could disrupt collections throughout the merged service.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: So Ayesha's central claim is that a merger would cut administrative costs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: An audit found that two councils saved twelve percent by jointly purchasing refuse bags and vehicle parts. That evidence supports merging the services because a larger authority could negotiate similar bulk discounts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha
utterances.text: Local authorities should merge neighbouring refuse-collection services. The administrative savings make that recommendation reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Moderator
utterances.text: In other words, the proposed policy is to combine neighbouring councils' refuse-collection services. Felix, you will have a final response after the break.

utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of all major demographic groups. Nkechi, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Clinical trials should be required to include equal numbers of participants from all major demographic groups because equal demographic representation can improve public trust in clinical research, especially among underrepresented communities.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Equal enrollment across major demographic groups is workable when trials use several recruitment sites, so that practicality is a reason to adopt the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: I disagree with the blanket rule. Equal quotas can make a trial unfair when the eligible patient population is not evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Some major demographic groups are routinely underrepresented in clinical research. That is a strong reason to require balanced enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: Soren has raised an issue about fairness, while the other guests have emphasized representativeness. Nkechi, what practical benefit would equal enrollment bring?

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: Equal enrollment gives researchers a better chance of detecting differences in treatment effects between demographic groups. That is why the requirement matters, rather than merely encouraging researchers to recruit widely.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: So you are saying that the proposal requires every major demographic group to have the same number of trial participants.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Soren's hospital serves a coastal region with an unusually old population.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: Recruitment targets can be monitored during a trial, making equal enrollment a realistic requirement. That feasibility is another reason to adopt the rule.

utterances.speaker: Esther
utterances.text: To sum up Nkechi's position, the central proposal is that clinical trials should enroll equal numbers from all major demographic groups.

utterances.speaker: Nkechi
utterances.text: By equal representation, I mean giving each major demographic group the same number of places in a trial.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: I have participated in three regulatory submissions.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: Clinical trials often use electronic data-capture systems.

utterances.speaker: Soren
utterances.text: Equal enrollment can identify differences in treatment effectiveness across demographic groups, which is another reason to support the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Gideon
utterances.text: The proposed rule is a requirement for balanced demographic enrollment rather than a suggestion to recruit broadly, which is another reason to support the central proposal.

utterances.speaker: Xavier
utterances.text: More reliable safety comparisons are another reason to require equal demographic enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice ballots let voters list candidates in order of preference. That feature gives each ballot more information than a single mark.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ballot transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority, ranked-choice counting can transfer a voter's ballot to the voter's next preferred candidate when the first choice is eliminated.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Those transfers can allow a remaining candidate to obtain a majority. This is a more demanding standard than merely receiving more votes than any individual rival.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Since a transferred ballot still expresses a voter's preference, a candidate who reaches a majority has support from more than half of participating voters.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That broader support gives the winner stronger democratic legitimacy. A majority-backed winner is easier to defend to constituents who preferred another candidate initially.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices would need to revise some ballot-counting software before adopting the system. That is a practical task, not a reason to preserve a weaker voting rule.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Plurality voting is preferable because its ballots are simpler for voters to complete. A single mark is undeniably familiar.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that simplicity does not make plurality voting preferable when ranked-choice instructions can be learned quickly. The familiar method can still produce a winner without majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A clear worked example and instructions enable voters to master ranked-choice voting quickly.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because voters can understand the procedure, a winner supported by more than half of participating voters has stronger democratic legitimacy. In other words, this is the same legitimacy advantage created by majority support.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I would want election officials to publish counting procedures before the first ranked-choice election.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Ranked-choice voting also reduces the risk that a spoiler candidate will distort the result. A candidate's presence need not force voters to abandon their genuine first choice.

utterances.speaker: Author

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because spoiler pressure is reduced, sincere voting becomes more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Because ranked-choice voting should replace plurality voting in legislative elections, reducing spoiler pressure makes sincere voting more attractive.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Election offices can archive each round of a ranked-choice count for public inspection.

utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether marathon organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. Dimitri, make the case for a ban.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Unequal access to drinks gives some runners a competitive advantage.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: Organisers should ban runners from using personal hydration support. The ban would create a more equal race because unequal access currently gives some runners an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Personal hydration teams give some runners access to drinks exactly when they want them.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: So you are saying that the fairness issue is unequal access to drinks. For context, the course has twelve official aid stations.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: No, personal hydration does not automatically give runners a competitive advantage. Most runners use it because official aid stations become crowded, and that is why they carry their own drinks.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: A ban would force every runner to depend on official aid stations. That dependence would lengthen queues at those stations.

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Those longer queues would make it harder for runners to maintain their pace.

utterances.speaker: Leopold
utterances.text: In other words, a ban would make race-day hydration less reliable.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: The studio clock is running fast.

utterances.speaker: Babajide
utterances.text: A blanket ban would ignore runners who need to carry drinks for medical reasons. Some medical conditions require runners to carry drinks themselves, which is why the ban would be unfair to them.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: A ban would improve fairness, which is a reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Organisers can require identical containers and limit handoffs to prevent personal hydration from creating an advantage.

utterances.speaker: Elif
utterances.text: Those safeguards can replace a blanket ban; that is why I reject the proposed ban.

utterances.text: Tonight's question: should senior managers spend a fixed proportion of their time mentoring junior employees? Zofia, you start.

utterances.text: But a fixed quota turns mentoring into box-ticking.

utterances.text: I back the fixed share, since explaining decisions to juniors sharpens a manager's own thinking. Our bank launched its scheme in 2019, I should say.

utterances.speaker: Nadia

utterances.speaker: Marisol

utterances.speaker: Marisol
utterances.text: The debate is being recorded for the evening news.

utterances.speaker: Hollis
utterances.text: My family has kept goats for three generations.

utterances.speaker: Elodie
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the question of enforcement after the break.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether health insurers should cover weight-loss medications for people who do not have diabetes. Gabriela, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Insurers should cover them, because obesity raises the risk of heart disease, joint failure and several cancers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Does the evidence show that the drugs work?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: In trials, patients lost around fifteen percent of their body weight, which is another reason to cover them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Harriet, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Coverage would cost insurers far more than they would save, since the medications cost over a thousand dollars a month.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jolene?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Most patients regain the weight within a year of stopping the medication.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: That is why coverage would mean paying indefinitely, and so it supports Harriet's point on cost.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: My aunt was prescribed one of these last spring, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gabriela, how do you answer the cost point?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: But preventing a heart attack or a joint replacement saves insurers far more than the drug costs.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I see, so you are saying the avoided treatment would offset the price of the medications.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Still, diet and exercise programmes do not work for many patients and are not far cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So where does that leave insurers?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quiet evening in the studio, I must say. Jolene, a last word.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So Harriet is saying insurers would be paying for these drugs indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Put another way, insurers should fund lifestyle programmes before medications.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether health insurers should cover weight-loss medications for people who do not have diabetes. Gabriela, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Insurers should cover them, because obesity raises the risk of heart disease, joint failure and several cancers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Does the evidence show that the drugs work?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: In trials, patients lost around fifteen percent of their body weight, which is another reason to cover them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Harriet, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Coverage would cost insurers far more than they would save, since the medications cost over a thousand dollars a month.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jolene?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Most patients regain the weight within a year of stopping the medication.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: That is why coverage would mean paying indefinitely, and so it supports Harriet's point on cost.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: My aunt was prescribed one of these last spring, as it happens.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gabriela, how do you answer the cost point?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: But averting a heart attack or a joint replacement saves insurers much more than the drug costs.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I see, so you are saying the avoided treatment would offset the price of the medications.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Still, diet and exercise programmes work for many patients and are far cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So where does that leave insurers?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quiet evening in the studio, I must say. Jolene, a last word.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So Harriet is saying insurers would be paying for these drugs indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Put another way, insurers should fund lifestyle programmes before medications.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Several of these medications are given as a weekly injection.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight's question: should councils ban petrol-powered leaf blowers on public land? Ifeoma, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Councils should ban them, because petrol blowers are far louder than electric ones.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Kieran, you disagree?

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: I do. A ban would leave parks departments struggling to clear wet leaves from big sites, since battery blowers run out within forty minutes.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Petrol blowers also throw out huge amounts of fine particulates, which is another reason to ban them.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: And that is a reason too: the workers who operate them breathe the exhaust all day.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: In other words, Sunita, operators are being harmed by the exhaust of their own machines.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: A ban would hit council budgets, because battery blowers cost three times as much as petrol ones.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: But the extra cost would be small, since councils already buy electric hedge trimmers in bulk at a discount.

utterances.speaker: Ifeoma
utterances.text: Kieran, what you say about wet leaves on big sites holds, because a ban would leave grounds crews without working equipment for big jobs.

utterances.speaker: Kieran
utterances.text: That is it. For the record, I ran a council grounds team for ten years.

utterances.speaker: Sunita
utterances.text: The council's grounds depot is next to the old station, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We will leave it there. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Tonight's question is whether new housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets. Noor, you support the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: New housing developments should meet mandatory minimum tree-canopy targets because trees reduce summer heat around them.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: I grew up on a treeless housing estate, so I understand why people want greenery nearby.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: In other words, Noor is arguing that mandatory canopy rules are justified by their cooling benefits.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: The city lost more than two hundred mature trees during housing construction last year. That is why the city should prevent housing construction from causing further tree loss.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Padraig, what is the strongest objection to a fixed target?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Planting trees during construction is cheaper than retrofitting them later, so developers can meet a tree-canopy target without major redesigns.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: The difficulty is that mandatory canopy targets can raise rents in smaller housing developments; for that reason, mandatory canopy targets should not apply to every housing development.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: So you are saying that affordability concerns outweigh protection from summer heat.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Developers can retain mature trees during construction.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Can the rule be adjusted rather than abandoned?

utterances.speaker: Noor
utterances.text: Phased canopy targets let builders preserve existing trees.

utterances.speaker: Odette
utterances.text: Put another way, phased canopy targets make the tree-canopy requirement workable.

utterances.speaker: Malik
utterances.text: Because developers can retain mature trees during construction, the city should publish canopy maps before approving housing projects. Those maps would identify areas where the city should require stronger canopy targets because they have little existing tree cover.

utterances.speaker: Padraig
utterances.text: My neighborhood association is holding its annual meeting next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: To sum up Malik's recommendation, he wants the city to require stronger canopy targets in areas with little existing tree cover.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Parties should face strict limits on total campaign spending, because without limits the richest ones can drown out every other voice in an election.

utterances.speaker: Renata

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Put another way, strict limits keep the contest fair.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: My local party once ran on a tiny budget and still won a council seat.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Limits would force parties to rely on volunteers and ideas rather than money, and that is why the contest would be fairer.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: If I follow you, capped budgets would make parties compete on ideas instead of advertising.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Still, limits set too low would protect incumbents, since they already enjoy name recognition without spending anything.

utterances.speaker: Renata
utterances.text: Fair enough. The next election is in October, so we should settle this soon.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Tonight we are discussing whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Annelise, you support the change.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Twice-yearly conferences let teachers discuss a student's progress in detail, which is why the replacement is worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My daughter has attended the same school since kindergarten. I am not convinced that a meeting can replace something families can read at home.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some teachers already spend their evenings preparing detailed comments for families. The new system would give families specific next steps, because a conversation can turn those comments into an actionable plan.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Those specific next steps would make it easier for families to support learning between meetings. That is why conferences could lead to more useful follow-up than a report card alone.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Maeve, what is your strongest objection to replacing the reports?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later. Because that record remains available after a meeting, schools should retain a written reporting system alongside any conferences.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Because specific next steps would make it easier for families to support learning between meetings, Annelise is proposing that schools use two parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards. Maeve, do you think the written record is essential?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, Maeve is saying that report cards offer parents a lasting written record. We will leave the audience to weigh that concern against the proposed follow-up benefits.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether phone operating systems should be forced to open up to rival app stores. Ulla, you start.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: They should, because a single store today controls which apps can be installed on nearly every phone. That is power no company should hold alone.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Is control the only problem?

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: No, the dominant stores take up to thirty percent of every sale. And competition between stores would push that commission down, which is another reason to require it.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid, your response.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: The closed stores keep users safe, since apps from unvetted stores are far more likely to contain malware.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Florin, you work in security.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: I do, and I say no to the idea, but not quite: forcing alternative stores would expose ordinary users to more malware, and I can't support a rule that does that.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So, Florin, you are saying the mandate would make phones less safe.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: Users who want a curated store could simply keep using the official one, because phone makers already allow sideloading on some devices without a rise in security incidents.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Rashid?

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Ulla, what you are saying is that people who want safety can stay with the official store, but most people never choose and just take defaults.

utterances.speaker: Ulla
utterances.text: By the way, my own phone is six years old, so I am hardly an early adopter.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Europe's digital markets regulation already requires alternative stores on some platforms. Small developers would also get a cheaper route to reach customers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: We are past the halfway mark, so final points please.

utterances.speaker: Rashid
utterances.text: Put simply, the safety of the official stores is the reason to keep them closed.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Welcome to the debate. Should youth football leagues prohibit heading until players reach sixteen? Dolores, you support the motion.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: Youth football leagues should prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen because repeated heading can cause cumulative effects from minor impacts.

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: A blanket prohibition on heading is unnecessary because trained coaches can teach safe heading technique without allowing heading in matches.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Players under sixteen need gradual preparation before they can head the ball safely, and gradual preparation can be provided through soft balls and controlled drills.

utterances.speaker: Imogen
utterances.text: A complete ban would prevent coaches from identifying players who need extra help with heading technique, since regular supervised practice helps coaches identify those players.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: Karima, does your alternative allow any heading in competitive matches?

utterances.speaker: Karima
utterances.text: The regional youth league introduced new concussion forms this season. That administrative change does not settle the question before us.

utterances.speaker: Florin
utterances.text: Youth leagues can permit carefully supervised heading before players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Dolores
utterances.text: In other words, a blanket prohibition on heading is unnecessary. That is my objection to the proposed ban. Separately, youth leagues can permit carefully supervised heading before players reach sixteen.

utterances.speaker: Isaac
utterances.text: The under-fourteen championship has twelve teams registered. We will now hear closing statements.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: The agenda item is whether we should turn vacant municipal buildings into affordable workspaces for small businesses. Petra, could you start with the building stock?

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: The municipality already owns several sound but vacant buildings. The municipality's building inventory includes photographs taken in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: Because the municipality already owns those buildings, converting the vacant municipal buildings would create affordable workspaces for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: The existing ownership is also important because the municipality could start renovating the buildings without purchasing additional land.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: Since the buildings are already municipal property, a municipal workspace program could keep rents below ordinary commercial rates.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: That same ownership shows that the municipality could pilot affordable workspaces across several neighbourhoods at once.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I worry that the proposal would mostly subsidise established companies rather than genuinely small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Petra
utterances.text: That objection is not right; in other words, converting the vacant municipal buildings would create affordable workspaces for small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Sanna
utterances.text: The next council meeting is scheduled for Thursday evening.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Tonight we ask whether health insurers should cover weight-loss medications for people who do not have diabetes. Gabriela, you start.

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: Insurers should cover them, because obesity raises the risk of heart disease, joint failure and several cancers.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Does the evidence show that the drugs work?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: In trials, patients lost around fifteen percent of their body weight, which is another reason to cover them.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Harriet, you disagree.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Coverage would cost insurers far more than they would save, since the medications cost over a thousand dollars a month.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Jolene?

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Most patients regain the weight within a year of stopping the medication.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: That is why coverage would mean paying indefinitely, and so it supports Harriet's point on cost.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: Gabriela, how do you answer the cost point?

utterances.speaker: Gabriela
utterances.text: But preventing a heart attack or a joint replacement saves insurers far more than the drug costs.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: I see, so you are saying the avoided treatment would offset the price of the medications.

utterances.speaker: Harriet
utterances.text: Still, diet and exercise programmes work for many patients and are far cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: So where does that leave insurers?

utterances.speaker: Host
utterances.text: A quiet evening in the studio, I must say. Jolene, a last word.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: So Harriet is saying insurers would be paying for these drugs indefinitely.

utterances.speaker: Jolene
utterances.text: Put another way, insurers should fund lifestyle programmes before medications.

props.text: Health insurers should cover weight-loss medications for people without diabetes.
Obesity raises the risk of heart disease, joint failure and several cancers.
In trials, patients on these medications lost around fifteen percent of their body weight.
Covering these medications would cost insurers far more than they would save.
The medications cost over a thousand dollars a month.
Most patients regain the weight within a year of stopping the medication.
Coverage would therefore mean paying indefinitely for these medications.
Preventing a heart attack or joint replacement saves insurers far more than the drug costs.
Insurers' savings from avoided treatment would offset the medications' cost.
Diet and exercise programmes work for many patients and are far cheaper than these medications.
Insurers should fund lifestyle programmes before medications.
The debate studio's audience has been unusually quiet this evening.
Jolene says that insurers would be paying for these medications indefinitely.
Lifestyle programmes should be tried first because the medications are so expensive.

utterances.speaker: Margit
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether low-income defendants should receive free legal representation in all civil eviction cases. Jasper, why do you support that policy?

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Low-income defendants often cannot afford a lawyer. For that reason, they should receive free legal representation in every civil eviction case.

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: I disagree with that approach. Providing free representation in every civil eviction case would lengthen hearings and increase court costs, but universal free legal representation is too broad.

utterances.speaker: Beatriz
utterances.text: Represented defendants are more likely to understand the filing deadlines in eviction proceedings, which is one reason the policy deserves support.

utterances.speaker: Jasper
utterances.text: Legal representation can prevent avoidable evictions caused by procedural mistakes. That is another reason to guarantee it in every civil eviction case.

utterances.speaker: Margit

utterances.speaker: Beatriz

utterances.speaker: Margit

utterances.speaker: Femi
utterances.text: Put another way, Jasper's position is that every low-income defendant facing civil eviction should have free legal representation.

utterances.speaker: Margit

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Tonight we are discussing whether schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Annelise, you support the change.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Schools should replace traditional report cards with twice-yearly parent-teacher conferences. Twice-yearly conferences let teachers discuss a student's progress in detail, which is why the replacement is worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: My daughter has attended the same school since kindergarten. I am not convinced that a meeting can replace something families can read at home.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Some teachers already spend their evenings preparing detailed comments for families. The new system would give families specific next steps, because a conversation can turn those comments into an actionable plan.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Those specific next steps would make it easier for families to support learning between meetings. That is why conferences could lead to more useful follow-up than a report card alone.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: Maeve, what is your strongest objection to replacing the reports?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later. Because that record remains available after a meeting, schools should keep a written reporting system in addition to any conferences.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: So Annelise is proposing that schools use two parent-teacher conferences instead of traditional report cards. Maeve, do you think the written record is essential?

utterances.speaker: Maeve
utterances.text: Yes. Traditional report cards provide a stable written record that parents can consult later.

utterances.speaker: Lucia
utterances.text: In other words, Maeve is saying that report cards offer parents a lasting written record. We will leave the audience to weigh that concern against the proposed follow-up benefits.
